articles.title: England v Pakistan: second men’s cricket Test, day two – as it happened
articles.summary: Ollie Robinson took 4-11 and Jofra Archer bowled ferociously as England dominated Pakistan’s batters and opened a 261-lead at Lord’s 62nd over: England 266-9 (Atkinson 38, Tongue 14) Scrap that: Atkinson takes a leg-bye off the second ball of this over. As Tongue prepares to face Abbas, the keeper, Mohammad Rizwan, calls for a helmet and goes up to the stumps – so Josh Tongue is now being treated like Joe Root. The ploy could backfire by making Tongue’s nicks harder for the slips to pick up. And it doesn’t seem to bother Tongue, who plays an uppish flick for a single to steal the strike. 61st over: England 264-9 (Atkinson 38, Tongue 13) Ali bowls to Atkinson, who promptly steps away to leg, dreaming of a six over backward point, but connects only with thin air. The over ends in a flurry of singles – one to each batter and then a tight one to Atkinson, who may have decided that he needs to protect Tongue from Abbas. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Joe Root did not want the England captaincy when the prospect started to be floated earlier this summer. After performing the role as a ­stand-in for the suspended Ben Stokes against New Zealand at the Oval, his father, Matt, floated a full-time return as a hypothetical and says this was met with a “no”.

Root was apparently swayed by the impending arrival of Stephen ­Fleming as head coach, with the pair speaking regularly before roles were locked down. But watching this ­one-sided second day against Pakistan at Lord’s – and indeed the ­one-sided series opener at ­Headingley – one wonders whether being handed the keys to this pace attack was another clincher for Root.

This has clearly been a stressful week for Root, with the needless Brydon Carse affair dominating the build-up and serving as an early reminder about the curve balls a Test captain can face. As per his old man, Root spent “four hours” on the phone last Sunday dealing with the fallout when he was meant to be relaxing at a family lunch. He was still thoroughly pissed off about it at his pre-match press conference two days later which, given his usual ­disposition, said plenty.

All that anger appeared to melt away at Lord’s on Friday, however, when, with 290 first innings runs on the board after some tail-end swish in the morning, Root’s attack set about unstitching Pakistan’s batting lineup once more. Ollie Robinson claimed a remarkable four for 11 from 13 overs, Jofra Archer three for 26 from 11.2. The visitors were bowled out for a sorry-looking 110 to ship a 180-run deficit – with England stretching this to 261 for the loss of three wickets in the final session.

I think [a lead of 261] is a lot of runs on this wicket. There was a ball with your name on it today.

[On Azan Awais] I’ve never seen someone play and miss so often and not get out. He’s obviously doing something right so fair play to him.

[On the four-man seam attack] I think I bowled 12 overs today, nine in the last game. I can probably play till 40 at this rate!

I don’t think the speedgun is accurate! It didn’t feel like [94.5mph] but I’ll take it.

Another plug for Simon Burnton’s piece on Azan Awais , who was left along on the burning deck when Pakistan batted.

The umpires have confirmed that we’re done for the day. And what a day it was for Ollie Robinson, who continued his extraordinary comeback by taking 4 for 11 in 13 overs.

That should be it for the day. If so, England will resume tomorrow*/on Sunday with a lead of 261 and a series win almost in the bag.

21st over: England 80-3 (Gay 30, Brook 6) Ali moves around the wicket to Gay, who watches an inswinger carefully onto the bat and times it through midwicket for four. Well played.

A rogue outswinger flies away for five wides, which takes England’s lead to 260.

20th over: England 71-3 (Gay 26, Brook 6) Gay ignores some wider deliveries from Abbas before edging a straighter one on the bounce to the keeper. He knows that, if he can survive until the close, batting should get easier – maybe not tomorrow, when the forecast is abysmal, but certainly on Sunday.

“It was my first experience playing in England,” said Azan Awais after scoring 98 off 170 for Pakistan Shaheens at Hove last summer, his first red-ball game in England. “The conditions are challenging for an opening batter, requiring patient survival early on.”

Those were certainly the conditions he faced at Lord’s 13 months later and those patient survival skills helped him build an innings much more impressive than a quick summary of his contribution – 46 runs scored before he top-edged a pull to deep square leg – might suggest.

However well the bowlers – Nathan Gilchrist, then of Kent and now of Warwickshire, and Hampshire’s Scott Currie – performed when opening up for the County Select XI last July, if that was a challenging situation that required patient survival, then facing Jofra Archer and Ollie Robinson toying with the Lord’s slope was another level entirely.

19th over: England 68-3 (Gay 25, Brook 4) Ali bowls a fine outswinger to Brook, who softens his hands to ensure an edge falls short of third slip. When Ali pulls his length back, Brook times an imperious boundary through point. “What. A. Shot,” purrs Dinesh Karthik in the commentary box.

Batting is seriously difficult now, with the floodlights on and the ball doing all sorts. Another outswinger from Ali beats Brook all ends up and whacks him high on the thigh.

18th over: England 64-3 (Gay 25, Brook 0) Mohammad Abbas is back on for Khurram Shahzad, who bowled a good spell of 8-1-26-2. Gay reaches to drive through extra cover for four, a shot of authority. He’s needed some luck – any batter would on this pitch – but his temperament has been excellent.

The light is fading so I don’t think the players will be on for much longer.

17th over: England 60-3 (Gay 21, Brook 0) A belter of a wicket maiden from Mohammad Ali.

Brook is not out! It was an instant, almost nonchalant review from Brook, which suggested he knew he’d inside-edged the ball onto the pad. And so he had.

Root is beaten by a vile lifter from Mohammad Ali and breaks into a familiar boyish smile. He’s not smiling when the next ball nips back to trap him plumb in front. Root wastes a review as well, a suggestion that his brain is more scrambled than usual. It was a fine delivery but LBWs are becoming a problem for Root: that’s the ninth in his last 12 Test innings.

16th over: England 60-2 (Gay 21, Root 24) A thick edge from Gay drops short of the slips and scuttles away for another boundary. England are scoring most of their runs in the V – the one at the other end of the pitch.

“What if Frank Hayes hadn’t played all nine of his Test matches against 1970s West Indies, having scored a century on debut?” writes Paul Mills. “He also once took 34 off an over from poor old Malcolm Nash.”

15th over: England 53-2 (Gay 16, Root 23) Root walks down the pitch to flick Ali into the leg side for two. It looks like a typical Root innings, 23 from 32 balls, but he’s hard to fight pretty hard. Gay has 16 from 44.

14th over: England 51-2 (Gay 16, Root 21) Another edge for four, this time when Gay reaches for a full, wide delivery from Khurram. England have had plenty of luck in this mini-session.

Play can continue for another hour and a half, but there’s a bit of rain forecast in around 45 minutes.

13th over: England 47-2 (Gay 12, Root 21) A wide yorker from Ali is squirted for four by Root, who then flashes another boundary past gully. It was at catchable height, a proper edge, but wide of the diving fielder.

12th over: England 39-2 (Gay 12, Root 13) Rizwan is not standing up to the stumps when Khurram or Mohammad Ali bowl to Root. That’s hard to fathom because Root has really struggled to deal with that tactic in the past 12 months.

Gay moves into double figures by cutting Khurram crisply for four. His temperament looks excellent and all those plays-and-misses, which are an occupational hazard on a pitch like this, don’t seem to have affected him.

11th over: England 34-2 (Gay 8, Root 12) Root bottom-edges the new bowler Mohammad Ali for three. Gay takes a risk by not running his bat in and is only just home when the throw hits the stumps. Careful now.

“Maybe it’s just me, but this summer I’ve noticed the absolute histrionics when a bowler is appealing for a wicket,” writes Bev. “I get enthusiasm, that’s fine, but lately it seems to be more dramatic than the RSC. What do people think?”

10th over: England 30-2 (Gay 8, Root 9) Eek, Emilio Gay is living dangerously. He’s beaten twice in that Khurram over – one loose shot, one good ball. This, by a distance, has been Khurram’s best spell of the series: 5-1-10-2.

“My what if is Tom Cartwright,” says Kim Thonger. “His nickname was Nail. The cricket writer Colin Bateman stated, ‘Cartwright was an exceptional bowler whose talents could not find a niche in the England side, much to the discredit of the selectors. His high, flowing action off a few steady paces produced unerring accuracy and nip for his rich assortment of seam and swing deliveries, but England looked usually for a first change bowler with extra pace.’ And Tom taught Ian Botham how to swing the ball at the end of his first-class career at Somerset.”

It’s hard to believe that somebody with Cartwright’s first-class record played only five Tests. I’d have to check but I think it was something like 1536 wickets at 19.11 apiece.

9th over: England 29-2 (Gay 8, Root 8) Mohammad Abbas screws his face up in confusion and disgust when Gay is beaten by a beautiful delivery. This Lord’s pitch is not to be trusted, not if you’re a batter.

8th over: England 27-2 (Gay 6, Root 8) Khurram drifts onto the pads of Root, who does the necessary through midwicke for his first boundary. The last couple of overs have been slightly calmer, even if the ball is still doing a bit. England lead by 207.

“Steven Finn would be my what if,” says Dominic Papineau. “Suffered being in a time when England valued control too much over raw wicket potential speed. I think it was Michael Holding lamenting Finn’s underuse when his stats were quoted with something like ‘all because they were worried about four an over’.”

The great sadness with Finn is that he fought back from being unselectable (sic) to bowl majestically against Australia and South Africa in 2015. He was still only 26 at that point, but injuries and self-doubt returned and eventually broke him.

With the obvious exception of Ben Hollioake, Finn might be my most poignant what if. My eyes were not entirely without moisture when I read the section in his book (which is superb) about the catharsis of his Ashes comeback at Edgbaston.

7th over: England 23-2 (Gay 6, Root 4) Gay releases a bit of the pressure with a pristine cover drive for four. He’s a good advert for weighted averages, because most of his Test appearances so far have been in extremely tough batting conditions.

6th over: England 18-2 (Gay 2, Root 3) Gay fences Khurram just short of the slips, who again look a bit too deep. He’s hanging in there, waiting for the new ball to lose its zing, but it’s seriously hard work. Khurram straightens a beauty past the edge later in the over.

“WinViz has England at 75%?!?” writes Michael Meagher. “That can’t be right!”

5th over: England 18-2 (Gay 2, Root 3) Root has to scramble to make his ground after being sent back by Gay. On that occasion it was the right call, but Gay’s running and calling in this short innings have been jittery.

Root is not out! Outside the line, next. Babar was reluctant to review and probably only did it because it was Root.

Pakistan review for LBW against Root! I think he’s outside the line, but it’s close: the keeper is up to the stumps so Root is stuck in his crease.

Yorkshire have escaped without charges from the Cricket Regulator after a formal investigation into a £1.75m payment the county made to a company controlled by the club’s chief executive, Sanjay Patel, for work on the sale of the Northern Superchargers Hundred franchise.

The Guardian revealed in June that the England and Wales Cricket Board was reviewing the consultancy fee, which related to the £100m sale of the Superchargers to the Sun Group last year, with the matter subsequently referred to the Cricket Regulator for a formal investigation.

Yorkshire’s 2025 accounts showed Patel’s company SMP73 Ltd received a commission of £1.75m for “corporate broker services in connection with the sale of Northern Superchargers Limited”, leading to concerns at Lord’s over the amount of money leaving the game and a possible conflict of interest.

Colin Graves, the Yorkshire chair, announced that the case had been dropped without charges being issued at a members forum at Scarborough on Thursday, which he confirmed in an email sent to supporters on Friday.

4th over: England 16-2 (Gay 2, Root 1) Cox’s wicket was the 21st to fall in only 108 overs of play. Out there I just don’t know what’s going off.

My kingdom for a decent hunch – it was comfortably out, hitting below the bails. Khurram Shahzad got one to nip back and hit the flap of the front pad as Cox tried in vain to bring down the curtain rail. He was a fair way back so the ball didn’t have too far to travel.

Pakistan review for LBW against Cox! Height is the issue; my hunch is umpire’s call and therefore not out.

3rd over: England 11-1 (Gay 0, Cox 11) Jordan Cox stands tall to punch England’s first boundary through point. That’s a lovely shot, really classy and controlled. So is Mohammad Abbas’s response, a seductive outswinger that beats the edge. And so is Cox’s response to the response, another measured square drive to the fence.

2nd over: England 4-1 (Gay 0, Cox 2) Khurram appeals for something and everything when Gay is hit on the thigh by an inswinger. Too high for LBW and there was no touch on the bat.

“What ifs,” begins Phil Harrison. “Simon Jones is obviously The One (could have been England’s Dale Steyn) but in Test terms, my other one is Jos Buttler. Sure, he did ok. And he’s still having a resplendent white-ball career. But I genuinely thought he might be England’s answer to Adam Gilchrist when he first emerged. A fresh-faced and cheerful destroyer, in all formats. I think he got in his own head a bit in Tests and I really wish he’d made it to the Stokes/McCullum era. They might have sorted him out.”

He definitely got in his own head too much; his interviews on the subject are fascinating.

Urgh, what a horrible dismissal. Duckett clouts a length ball from Khurram Shahzad straight to mid-off, where Babar Azam takes a simple catch.

1st over: England 1-0 (Duckett 1, Gay 0) An accurate first over from Mohammad Abbas. Duckett plays tip and run to get off the mark; Gay tries to do likewise but it’s a bit tighter and Duckett sends him back.

The sun is out and the players are back on the field. Emilio Gay could do with a few runs after a tough spell; his last five Test innings have yielded 62 runs.

Andy Flintoff has emailed the correct answer , which is kind of appropriate.

Was it Grievous Bodily Harmison’s 7-12 against the West Indies in 2004?

David Hopkins also got it, but he doesn’t share a name with Harmy’s best mate.

I forgot to say that the umpires have brought tea forward due to the change of innings. That means we’ll have an evening session of just under three hours.

“Derek Underwood?” suggests Peter in response to the question a couple of entries ago. Underwood did manage it against New Zealand in 1971 (11.6-7-12-6 in the days of eight-ball overs), but there have been a few examples since then.

It happened five times in 1978 (Phil Edmonds x 3, Chris Old and Bob Willis). Since then there have been three instances: Ollie Robinson today, Lord Beefy’s rampage at Edgbaston in 1981… and another famous rampage by an England fast bowler.

“My ‘what if’ is Ben Foakes,” says Max Willians. “There’s a world not different to this one where he has 100 caps and series wins against India and Australia. Also Haseeb Hameed. But still optimistic he comes again.”

Ah yes, Hameed is a really good one. In my time preparing to be murdered by Claude, I’ve seen only four England cricketers who I was 100.00% certain would make it: Stuart Broad, Joe Root, Haseeb Hameed and Jacob Bethell.

Pop quiz, hotshot Right, shut up, stop talking to Claude and answer this niche question. Ollie Robinson finished with outrageous figures of 13-6-11-4.

Before today, who was the last England bowler to take at least four wickets in a Test innings while conceding less than one run per over?

Jofra Archer cleans up Mohammad Abbas to complete a marvellous bowling performance. They lead by 180 runs and are apparently cruising towards a series victory.

Archer ends with figures of 11.2-1-26-3, and they don’t flatter him. Pretty soon he is going to bulldoze a team.

37th over: Pakistan 110-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 3) “‘Right, where were we?’” begins John Burton, quoting Claude’s earlier OBO. “I can’t be the only one who instantly heard that in a John Arlott burr, can I?”

Oh yes, good one. I can also hear Johnners saying it. (Brian, not Emma.)

36th over: Pakistan 109-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 3) Ali is dropped by Root at leg slip, a tough chance as he flew to his right. Jofra Archer’s frustration continues when Ali survives an LBW review after playing around a beautiful inswinger. It was not out on the field and umpire’s call on impact.

35th over: Pakistan 107-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 1) Imam-ul-Haq will not bat because of his calf injury, so Mohammad Abbas and Muhammad Ali are Pakistan’s last pair. Robinson would love another five-for to continue his fairytale return; he almost gets it when Abbas inside-edges just past the stumps.

Since his recall, Robinson has taken 19 wickets at 8.78 apiece. Conditions have been favourable, sure, but that’s über-Lohmann stuff . Or maybe it should be unter-Lohmann.

Ollie Robinson has bounced out Azan Awais! With only the rabbits for company, Awais decided to take on the short ball and hopefully bring up his fifty in the process. Instead he clothed it towards deep square and was comfortably caught by Emilio Gay.

Ollie Robinson hoovers up another wicket. Khurram fences at a good delivery and is smartly taken in the slips by Harry Brook. Robinson has 3 for 8 in 11.2 overs, and England’s 2025-26 Ashes campaign is getting worse by the minute.

34th over: Pakistan 105-6 (Azan 46, Khurram 1) Khurram Shahzad faces his first ball from somewhere near square leg and is hit on the pad. “Where’s he going?!” chuckles Mark Wood on commentary.

When Khurram takes a single, Archer beats Azan twice in a row. Apparently Azan has played and missed at Archer 14 times today.

“Hi Rob,” writes Tom Paternoster-Howe, “old Claude hasn’t quite got it right. There’s no mention of the Judge, nor reference to an obscure, but delightful, old scorecard.

“For the rest, though, the tone is pretty much spot-on. That must be a bit of a frightening harbinger of obsolescence, not unlike walking in a graveyard and seeing a headstone with your name on it. All the best with your inevitable existential crisis.”

And it’s goodnight from Ali Usman. He played a nothing shot at a shortish delivery at Archer and dragged the ball back onto the stumps.

33rd over: Pakistan 104-5 (Azan 46, Usman 1) Robinson beats Usman with successive deliveries, the first a bona fide jaffa. Usman walks down the track in response, so Smith moves back up to the stumps – and the next ball swings past him for four byes. Robinson’s figures are exceptional (11-6-8-2) but at least 12 byes have been conceded on his watch. Look, it’s complicated.

“Feels like Ollie Robinson slots next to Ben Foakes as players who should’ve had 50+ caps already,” says Max Williams. “Hopefully he bowls us to the Ashes next summer. Who are your biggest What If players for England?”

Blimey, at least buy me dinner tell me yours first. There are so many, from Mark Ramprakash (52 caps) to Duncan Spencer (0). I suspect the biggest for many people would be Simon Jones. But if we’re talking purely about selection, I’d probably say Ramps. Claude reckons the biggest ‘what if’ is Dermot Munton.

32nd over: Pakistan 99-5 (Azan 46, Usman 1) Joe Root’s infectious, mischievous smile is on display when he sees a replay of Ollie Robinson slipping in the field. His joie de vivre has somehow survived 14 years in international cricket.

“I noticed the anonymous OBO emailer in over 18 was cautious about getting into trouble at work for reading the OBO during working hours,” writes John Starbuck. “Although I’m now retired, one of my roles in a large public sector outfit was monitoring staff IT misdeeds, but I’d not shop anyone for following the OBO because what else can you do?”

31st over: Pakistan 95-5 (Azan 43, Usman 0) Still no sign of Imam-ul-Haq, who has a calf problem, so Ali Usman comes in at No7. His first ball seams and lifts violently to beat the edge, hit Smith on the thumb and fly away for four byes. Smith walks away in pain, then walks back to a traditional wicketkeeping position. No need to be up to the stumps for Usman, who is a decent No9 but no more.

Robinson’s bowling figures have been nicked from Curtly Ambrose: 10-5-8-2. And his career bowling average has dropped to 20.50: the best of any England bowler with 50 Test wickets since Frank Tyson in the 1950s.

“I think your job’s safe enough...” writes Barney. “Quite a few things wrong with that paragraph from Claude. England are batting, but Archer is bowling. It’s apparently a Test match, but we’re calculating the run rate - when the seven wickets down looks like more of an issue. If it is a one day game, then England have three overs to score 114. I’m not sure why anyone would be worrying about tea. Keep up the human work.”

You’re right, of course you are. But my mind’s ear has been hijacked by a single phrase: my kingdom for a Twix!

Ollie Robinson’s done it again! There was no inside edge and the ball wouild have hit the top of the stumps, so Rizwan is on his way and Joe Root has struck gold with two risky reviews in the last half an hour.

England review for LBW against Rizwan! Hmm, not sure about this. It was a beautiful nipbacker there might be an inside edge and height could be an issue.
paragraphs: Joe Root did not want the England captaincy when the prospect started to be floated earlier this summer. After performing the role as a ­stand-in for the suspended Ben Stokes against New Zealand at the Oval, his father, Matt, floated a full-time return as a hypothetical and says this was met with a “no”.

Root was apparently swayed by the impending arrival of Stephen ­Fleming as head coach, with the pair speaking regularly before roles were locked down. But watching this ­one-sided second day against Pakistan at Lord’s – and indeed the ­one-sided series opener at ­Headingley – one wonders whether being handed the keys to this pace attack was another clincher for Root.

This has clearly been a stressful week for Root, with the needless Brydon Carse affair dominating the build-up and serving as an early reminder about the curve balls a Test captain can face. As per his old man, Root spent “four hours” on the phone last Sunday dealing with the fallout when he was meant to be relaxing at a family lunch. He was still thoroughly pissed off about it at his pre-match press conference two days later which, given his usual ­disposition, said plenty.

All that anger appeared to melt away at Lord’s on Friday, however, when, with 290 first innings runs on the board after some tail-end swish in the morning, Root’s attack set about unstitching Pakistan’s batting lineup once more. Ollie Robinson claimed a remarkable four for 11 from 13 overs, Jofra Archer three for 26 from 11.2. The visitors were bowled out for a sorry-looking 110 to ship a 180-run deficit – with England stretching this to 261 for the loss of three wickets in the final session.
I think [a lead of 261] is a lot of runs on this wicket. There was a ball with your name on it today.
[On Azan Awais] I’ve never seen someone play and miss so often and not get out. He’s obviously doing something right so fair play to him.
[On the four-man seam attack] I think I bowled 12 overs today, nine in the last game. I can probably play till 40 at this rate!
I don’t think the speedgun is accurate! It didn’t feel like [94.5mph] but I’ll take it.
Another plug for Simon Burnton’s piece on Azan Awais , who was left along on the burning deck when Pakistan batted.
The umpires have confirmed that we’re done for the day. And what a day it was for Ollie Robinson, who continued his extraordinary comeback by taking 4 for 11 in 13 overs.
That should be it for the day. If so, England will resume tomorrow*/on Sunday with a lead of 261 and a series win almost in the bag.
21st over: England 80-3 (Gay 30, Brook 6) Ali moves around the wicket to Gay, who watches an inswinger carefully onto the bat and times it through midwicket for four. Well played.
A rogue outswinger flies away for five wides, which takes England’s lead to 260.

20th over: England 71-3 (Gay 26, Brook 6) Gay ignores some wider deliveries from Abbas before edging a straighter one on the bounce to the keeper. He knows that, if he can survive until the close, batting should get easier – maybe not tomorrow, when the forecast is abysmal, but certainly on Sunday.

“It was my first experience playing in England,” said Azan Awais after scoring 98 off 170 for Pakistan Shaheens at Hove last summer, his first red-ball game in England. “The conditions are challenging for an opening batter, requiring patient survival early on.”

Those were certainly the conditions he faced at Lord’s 13 months later and those patient survival skills helped him build an innings much more impressive than a quick summary of his contribution – 46 runs scored before he top-edged a pull to deep square leg – might suggest.

However well the bowlers – Nathan Gilchrist, then of Kent and now of Warwickshire, and Hampshire’s Scott Currie – performed when opening up for the County Select XI last July, if that was a challenging situation that required patient survival, then facing Jofra Archer and Ollie Robinson toying with the Lord’s slope was another level entirely.

19th over: England 68-3 (Gay 25, Brook 4) Ali bowls a fine outswinger to Brook, who softens his hands to ensure an edge falls short of third slip. When Ali pulls his length back, Brook times an imperious boundary through point. “What. A. Shot,” purrs Dinesh Karthik in the commentary box.
Batting is seriously difficult now, with the floodlights on and the ball doing all sorts. Another outswinger from Ali beats Brook all ends up and whacks him high on the thigh.

18th over: England 64-3 (Gay 25, Brook 0) Mohammad Abbas is back on for Khurram Shahzad, who bowled a good spell of 8-1-26-2. Gay reaches to drive through extra cover for four, a shot of authority. He’s needed some luck – any batter would on this pitch – but his temperament has been excellent.
The light is fading so I don’t think the players will be on for much longer.
17th over: England 60-3 (Gay 21, Brook 0) A belter of a wicket maiden from Mohammad Ali.
Brook is not out! It was an instant, almost nonchalant review from Brook, which suggested he knew he’d inside-edged the ball onto the pad. And so he had.

Root is beaten by a vile lifter from Mohammad Ali and breaks into a familiar boyish smile. He’s not smiling when the next ball nips back to trap him plumb in front. Root wastes a review as well, a suggestion that his brain is more scrambled than usual. It was a fine delivery but LBWs are becoming a problem for Root: that’s the ninth in his last 12 Test innings.

16th over: England 60-2 (Gay 21, Root 24) A thick edge from Gay drops short of the slips and scuttles away for another boundary. England are scoring most of their runs in the V – the one at the other end of the pitch.

“What if Frank Hayes hadn’t played all nine of his Test matches against 1970s West Indies, having scored a century on debut?” writes Paul Mills. “He also once took 34 off an over from poor old Malcolm Nash.”

15th over: England 53-2 (Gay 16, Root 23) Root walks down the pitch to flick Ali into the leg side for two. It looks like a typical Root innings, 23 from 32 balls, but he’s hard to fight pretty hard. Gay has 16 from 44.
14th over: England 51-2 (Gay 16, Root 21) Another edge for four, this time when Gay reaches for a full, wide delivery from Khurram. England have had plenty of luck in this mini-session.
Play can continue for another hour and a half, but there’s a bit of rain forecast in around 45 minutes.

13th over: England 47-2 (Gay 12, Root 21) A wide yorker from Ali is squirted for four by Root, who then flashes another boundary past gully. It was at catchable height, a proper edge, but wide of the diving fielder.

12th over: England 39-2 (Gay 12, Root 13) Rizwan is not standing up to the stumps when Khurram or Mohammad Ali bowl to Root. That’s hard to fathom because Root has really struggled to deal with that tactic in the past 12 months.

Gay moves into double figures by cutting Khurram crisply for four. His temperament looks excellent and all those plays-and-misses, which are an occupational hazard on a pitch like this, don’t seem to have affected him.

11th over: England 34-2 (Gay 8, Root 12) Root bottom-edges the new bowler Mohammad Ali for three. Gay takes a risk by not running his bat in and is only just home when the throw hits the stumps. Careful now.

“Maybe it’s just me, but this summer I’ve noticed the absolute histrionics when a bowler is appealing for a wicket,” writes Bev. “I get enthusiasm, that’s fine, but lately it seems to be more dramatic than the RSC. What do people think?”

10th over: England 30-2 (Gay 8, Root 9) Eek, Emilio Gay is living dangerously. He’s beaten twice in that Khurram over – one loose shot, one good ball. This, by a distance, has been Khurram’s best spell of the series: 5-1-10-2.

“My what if is Tom Cartwright,” says Kim Thonger. “His nickname was Nail. The cricket writer Colin Bateman stated, ‘Cartwright was an exceptional bowler whose talents could not find a niche in the England side, much to the discredit of the selectors. His high, flowing action off a few steady paces produced unerring accuracy and nip for his rich assortment of seam and swing deliveries, but England looked usually for a first change bowler with extra pace.’ And Tom taught Ian Botham how to swing the ball at the end of his first-class career at Somerset.”
It’s hard to believe that somebody with Cartwright’s first-class record played only five Tests. I’d have to check but I think it was something like 1536 wickets at 19.11 apiece.

9th over: England 29-2 (Gay 8, Root 8) Mohammad Abbas screws his face up in confusion and disgust when Gay is beaten by a beautiful delivery. This Lord’s pitch is not to be trusted, not if you’re a batter.

8th over: England 27-2 (Gay 6, Root 8) Khurram drifts onto the pads of Root, who does the necessary through midwicke for his first boundary. The last couple of overs have been slightly calmer, even if the ball is still doing a bit. England lead by 207.

“Steven Finn would be my what if,” says Dominic Papineau. “Suffered being in a time when England valued control too much over raw wicket potential speed. I think it was Michael Holding lamenting Finn’s underuse when his stats were quoted with something like ‘all because they were worried about four an over’.”

The great sadness with Finn is that he fought back from being unselectable (sic) to bowl majestically against Australia and South Africa in 2015. He was still only 26 at that point, but injuries and self-doubt returned and eventually broke him.

With the obvious exception of Ben Hollioake, Finn might be my most poignant what if. My eyes were not entirely without moisture when I read the section in his book (which is superb) about the catharsis of his Ashes comeback at Edgbaston.

7th over: England 23-2 (Gay 6, Root 4) Gay releases a bit of the pressure with a pristine cover drive for four. He’s a good advert for weighted averages, because most of his Test appearances so far have been in extremely tough batting conditions.

6th over: England 18-2 (Gay 2, Root 3) Gay fences Khurram just short of the slips, who again look a bit too deep. He’s hanging in there, waiting for the new ball to lose its zing, but it’s seriously hard work. Khurram straightens a beauty past the edge later in the over.
“WinViz has England at 75%?!?” writes Michael Meagher. “That can’t be right!”

5th over: England 18-2 (Gay 2, Root 3) Root has to scramble to make his ground after being sent back by Gay. On that occasion it was the right call, but Gay’s running and calling in this short innings have been jittery.
Root is not out! Outside the line, next. Babar was reluctant to review and probably only did it because it was Root.
Pakistan review for LBW against Root! I think he’s outside the line, but it’s close: the keeper is up to the stumps so Root is stuck in his crease.

Yorkshire have escaped without charges from the Cricket Regulator after a formal investigation into a £1.75m payment the county made to a company controlled by the club’s chief executive, Sanjay Patel, for work on the sale of the Northern Superchargers Hundred franchise.

The Guardian revealed in June that the England and Wales Cricket Board was reviewing the consultancy fee, which related to the £100m sale of the Superchargers to the Sun Group last year, with the matter subsequently referred to the Cricket Regulator for a formal investigation.

Yorkshire’s 2025 accounts showed Patel’s company SMP73 Ltd received a commission of £1.75m for “corporate broker services in connection with the sale of Northern Superchargers Limited”, leading to concerns at Lord’s over the amount of money leaving the game and a possible conflict of interest.

Colin Graves, the Yorkshire chair, announced that the case had been dropped without charges being issued at a members forum at Scarborough on Thursday, which he confirmed in an email sent to supporters on Friday.
4th over: England 16-2 (Gay 2, Root 1) Cox’s wicket was the 21st to fall in only 108 overs of play. Out there I just don’t know what’s going off.

My kingdom for a decent hunch – it was comfortably out, hitting below the bails. Khurram Shahzad got one to nip back and hit the flap of the front pad as Cox tried in vain to bring down the curtain rail. He was a fair way back so the ball didn’t have too far to travel.
Pakistan review for LBW against Cox! Height is the issue; my hunch is umpire’s call and therefore not out.

3rd over: England 11-1 (Gay 0, Cox 11) Jordan Cox stands tall to punch England’s first boundary through point. That’s a lovely shot, really classy and controlled. So is Mohammad Abbas’s response, a seductive outswinger that beats the edge. And so is Cox’s response to the response, another measured square drive to the fence.
2nd over: England 4-1 (Gay 0, Cox 2) Khurram appeals for something and everything when Gay is hit on the thigh by an inswinger. Too high for LBW and there was no touch on the bat.

“What ifs,” begins Phil Harrison. “Simon Jones is obviously The One (could have been England’s Dale Steyn) but in Test terms, my other one is Jos Buttler. Sure, he did ok. And he’s still having a resplendent white-ball career. But I genuinely thought he might be England’s answer to Adam Gilchrist when he first emerged. A fresh-faced and cheerful destroyer, in all formats. I think he got in his own head a bit in Tests and I really wish he’d made it to the Stokes/McCullum era. They might have sorted him out.”
He definitely got in his own head too much; his interviews on the subject are fascinating.
Urgh, what a horrible dismissal. Duckett clouts a length ball from Khurram Shahzad straight to mid-off, where Babar Azam takes a simple catch.

1st over: England 1-0 (Duckett 1, Gay 0) An accurate first over from Mohammad Abbas. Duckett plays tip and run to get off the mark; Gay tries to do likewise but it’s a bit tighter and Duckett sends him back.
The sun is out and the players are back on the field. Emilio Gay could do with a few runs after a tough spell; his last five Test innings have yielded 62 runs.
Andy Flintoff has emailed the correct answer , which is kind of appropriate.
Was it Grievous Bodily Harmison’s 7-12 against the West Indies in 2004?
David Hopkins also got it, but he doesn’t share a name with Harmy’s best mate.
I forgot to say that the umpires have brought tea forward due to the change of innings. That means we’ll have an evening session of just under three hours.

“Derek Underwood?” suggests Peter in response to the question a couple of entries ago. Underwood did manage it against New Zealand in 1971 (11.6-7-12-6 in the days of eight-ball overs), but there have been a few examples since then.

It happened five times in 1978 (Phil Edmonds x 3, Chris Old and Bob Willis). Since then there have been three instances: Ollie Robinson today, Lord Beefy’s rampage at Edgbaston in 1981… and another famous rampage by an England fast bowler.

“My ‘what if’ is Ben Foakes,” says Max Willians. “There’s a world not different to this one where he has 100 caps and series wins against India and Australia. Also Haseeb Hameed. But still optimistic he comes again.”

Ah yes, Hameed is a really good one. In my time preparing to be murdered by Claude, I’ve seen only four England cricketers who I was 100.00% certain would make it: Stuart Broad, Joe Root, Haseeb Hameed and Jacob Bethell.
Pop quiz, hotshot Right, shut up, stop talking to Claude and answer this niche question. Ollie Robinson finished with outrageous figures of 13-6-11-4.
Before today, who was the last England bowler to take at least four wickets in a Test innings while conceding less than one run per over?
Jofra Archer cleans up Mohammad Abbas to complete a marvellous bowling performance. They lead by 180 runs and are apparently cruising towards a series victory.
Archer ends with figures of 11.2-1-26-3, and they don’t flatter him. Pretty soon he is going to bulldoze a team.
37th over: Pakistan 110-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 3) “‘Right, where were we?’” begins John Burton, quoting Claude’s earlier OBO. “I can’t be the only one who instantly heard that in a John Arlott burr, can I?”
Oh yes, good one. I can also hear Johnners saying it. (Brian, not Emma.)

36th over: Pakistan 109-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 3) Ali is dropped by Root at leg slip, a tough chance as he flew to his right. Jofra Archer’s frustration continues when Ali survives an LBW review after playing around a beautiful inswinger. It was not out on the field and umpire’s call on impact.

35th over: Pakistan 107-8 (Abbas 1, Ali 1) Imam-ul-Haq will not bat because of his calf injury, so Mohammad Abbas and Muhammad Ali are Pakistan’s last pair. Robinson would love another five-for to continue his fairytale return; he almost gets it when Abbas inside-edges just past the stumps.
Since his recall, Robinson has taken 19 wickets at 8.78 apiece. Conditions have been favourable, sure, but that’s über-Lohmann stuff . Or maybe it should be unter-Lohmann.

Ollie Robinson has bounced out Azan Awais! With only the rabbits for company, Awais decided to take on the short ball and hopefully bring up his fifty in the process. Instead he clothed it towards deep square and was comfortably caught by Emilio Gay.

Ollie Robinson hoovers up another wicket. Khurram fences at a good delivery and is smartly taken in the slips by Harry Brook. Robinson has 3 for 8 in 11.2 overs, and England’s 2025-26 Ashes campaign is getting worse by the minute.
34th over: Pakistan 105-6 (Azan 46, Khurram 1) Khurram Shahzad faces his first ball from somewhere near square leg and is hit on the pad. “Where’s he going?!” chuckles Mark Wood on commentary.
When Khurram takes a single, Archer beats Azan twice in a row. Apparently Azan has played and missed at Archer 14 times today.
“Hi Rob,” writes Tom Paternoster-Howe, “old Claude hasn’t quite got it right. There’s no mention of the Judge, nor reference to an obscure, but delightful, old scorecard.

“For the rest, though, the tone is pretty much spot-on. That must be a bit of a frightening harbinger of obsolescence, not unlike walking in a graveyard and seeing a headstone with your name on it. All the best with your inevitable existential crisis.”
And it’s goodnight from Ali Usman. He played a nothing shot at a shortish delivery at Archer and dragged the ball back onto the stumps.

33rd over: Pakistan 104-5 (Azan 46, Usman 1) Robinson beats Usman with successive deliveries, the first a bona fide jaffa. Usman walks down the track in response, so Smith moves back up to the stumps – and the next ball swings past him for four byes. Robinson’s figures are exceptional (11-6-8-2) but at least 12 byes have been conceded on his watch. Look, it’s complicated.

“Feels like Ollie Robinson slots next to Ben Foakes as players who should’ve had 50+ caps already,” says Max Williams. “Hopefully he bowls us to the Ashes next summer. Who are your biggest What If players for England?”

Blimey, at least buy me dinner tell me yours first. There are so many, from Mark Ramprakash (52 caps) to Duncan Spencer (0). I suspect the biggest for many people would be Simon Jones. But if we’re talking purely about selection, I’d probably say Ramps. Claude reckons the biggest ‘what if’ is Dermot Munton.

32nd over: Pakistan 99-5 (Azan 46, Usman 1) Joe Root’s infectious, mischievous smile is on display when he sees a replay of Ollie Robinson slipping in the field. His joie de vivre has somehow survived 14 years in international cricket.

“I noticed the anonymous OBO emailer in over 18 was cautious about getting into trouble at work for reading the OBO during working hours,” writes John Starbuck. “Although I’m now retired, one of my roles in a large public sector outfit was monitoring staff IT misdeeds, but I’d not shop anyone for following the OBO because what else can you do?”

31st over: Pakistan 95-5 (Azan 43, Usman 0) Still no sign of Imam-ul-Haq, who has a calf problem, so Ali Usman comes in at No7. His first ball seams and lifts violently to beat the edge, hit Smith on the thumb and fly away for four byes. Smith walks away in pain, then walks back to a traditional wicketkeeping position. No need to be up to the stumps for Usman, who is a decent No9 but no more.

Robinson’s bowling figures have been nicked from Curtly Ambrose: 10-5-8-2. And his career bowling average has dropped to 20.50: the best of any England bowler with 50 Test wickets since Frank Tyson in the 1950s.

“I think your job’s safe enough...” writes Barney. “Quite a few things wrong with that paragraph from Claude. England are batting, but Archer is bowling. It’s apparently a Test match, but we’re calculating the run rate - when the seven wickets down looks like more of an issue. If it is a one day game, then England have three overs to score 114. I’m not sure why anyone would be worrying about tea. Keep up the human work.”
You’re right, of course you are. But my mind’s ear has been hijacked by a single phrase: my kingdom for a Twix!

Ollie Robinson’s done it again! There was no inside edge and the ball wouild have hit the top of the stumps, so Rizwan is on his way and Joe Root has struck gold with two risky reviews in the last half an hour.
England review for LBW against Rizwan! Hmm, not sure about this. It was a beautiful nipbacker there might be an inside edge and height could be an issue.

articles.title: Emery and Watkins ‘shed tears’ saying goodbye; transfer latest; Celtic and Rangers punished: football – as it happened
articles.summary: All the latest press conference news, transfer latest and buildup to the weekend’s fixtures Premier League things to look out for Brighton women’s manager Dario Vidosic said of his time at the club: I have loved my time at the Albion and am proud of what we have achieved together. Leaving has been a difficult decision, but I believe it is the right time for me and my family to begin a new chapter. I would like to thank the players, staff and supporters for their support throughout my time at the club and wish everyone associated with Albion every success in the future. Continue reading...
articles.content:
That’s all we have time for on this blog . Thank you for reading and for your emails. I’ll leave you with The Talk, a handy round-up of some of the best Friday newslines

Oh, and I am now helming our minute-by-minute report of today’s Premier League clash: Crystal Palace v Manchester City (8pm BST kick-off). Join me!

Not a sentence I thought I would be typing today : Álvaro Morata has joined Spanish second-division side Leganés, on loan from Italian side Como! The veteran striker, 33, Morata played 26 matches in Serie A last season as Como qualified for the Champions League, a competition he won twice with Real Madrid.

Leganés said on their website they would have “an option to buy [Morata] at the end of the season”.

It is not the fixture that Derek McInnes would have wanted following Rangers’ disastrous penalty-shootout defeat in their Conference League qualifier at Jablonec in the Czech Republic, but the Glasgow side head to Pittodrie for a tough away day at Aberdeen on Sunday. The Ibrox club had earlier been eliminated from the Europa League by Jagiellonia Bialystok and Rangers have won just two of their seven games this season under McInnes.

Lawrence Shankland, the newly-appointed captain following his summer move from Hearts, has said this of Rangers’ European heartache:

There’s been plenty of low moments in football, but this is certainly one that’s right up there in terms of how bad it feels. This is a real tough blow but we need to stick together, we need to find it in ourselves to have that togetherness and that’s hard at times like this, because you can tend to go on as an individual and look after number one and we can’t have that in the difficult times. We need to try and stick together as a team and rally around each other. Over two legs it wasn’t good enough.

We’ll need to go and watch it back, but there were times in the second half that they were causing us a lot of problems and we just didn’t get to grips with the game at all. In terms of moments, it probably felt like they were the team that were going to have one and we never did done enough at the top end to create a clear-cut chance or have that moment, and that’s disappointing.

Cole Palmer is genuinely unusual in the modern game . He turns up in strange spaces, finds gullies and currents in between those static pegs. Right now he is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there, in the sense of inventing the game in front of him, dishing up in those moments the pure pleasure of a story being told in real time.

He even looks a little unusual in an era of hyper-athletes. Palmer is light and mobile. He can turn with balletic grace. But he also has that gangly, mischievous physicality, like a very clever cartoon alpaca has worked out how to put on a royal blue football kit and run around occasionally doing amusing celebrations.

Brighton have confirmed the appointment of Arturo Ruiz from Real Sociedad as a replacement head coach for Dario Vidosic.

The Women’s Super League club have acted quickly to replace Vidosic, whose departure was confirmed earlier on Friday, just over a week before the start of the new Women’s Super League campaign. Vidosic is understood to be the leading candidate for the head coach role at the NWSL side Angel City and although Brighton are disappointed to lose the Croatia-born Australian, they are understood to be very happy to be able to bring in Ruiz on a three-year deal, subject to a work permit being finalised.

More bad news for Crystal Palace after the London side lost Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea and Chadi Riad during last weekend’s 2-0 defeat at Everton. Now a deal for Club Brugge defender Joel Ordóñez, could be called off after reported complications with the centre-back’s medical.

Palace looked like they had beaten Aston Villa to the signing of Ordóñez, who is recovering from a broken metatarsal. But it looks like the injury is worse than it was initially thought to be.

Manchester United have signed the Sweden winger Monica Jusu Bah from the Swedish side BK Häcken on a deal until June 2030, for an undisclosed fee reportedly in excess of £400,000. The 23-year-old helped Häcken lift last season’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup. She told Manchester United’s website: “It’s an unbelievable feeling to join Manchester United. There is a real togetherness in the group, and you can feel the excitement from everyone, for a big season ahead. “The opportunity to work with Eva Olid is perfect, everybody knows the quality of her coaching and her ability to support players to reach their highest level. I’m ready to keep pushing myself, help the team achieve our ambitions together and create special memories at this incredible club.”

That is a name I haven’t heard in a while. Was part of that famous Valencia side and good on Championship Manager, if I remember correctly.

González, 52, has ⁠a close relationship with ​Lionel ​Messi, which I imagine is a huge reason for his appointment. He previously has served ​as the head coach ​at ‌Argentine sides ​Rosario ​Central, Union (Santa Fe) and Platense.

A bit more from Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi, who wants one more signing despite Spurs already spending around £300m this summer.

I didn’t expect a market like we have done,” De Zerbi said. “I think we can do one player more and in one specific position. Yesterday we went for dinner with the owner, with Vinai [Venkatesham, the chief executive], with Johan [Lange, the sporting director] and with Enrico [Venturelli, De Zerbi’s assistant]. We spoke about this but we have all of us on the same page and there is a very good connection.

It can be possible out or in. The transfer market is crazy and we have to be able to find the new players. If some players go out, leave, or to make another player [come] in … I don’t know. We are very happy with the market we have done until now. It has been more than my expectation at the beginning.”

I understand why Tottenham spent money on Omar Marmoush – Richarlison and Dominic Solanke are not reliable for form and fitness – but I can’t really get my head around Spurs spent £75m on Savinho/Sávio , given they already have Mohammed Kudus and Deki Kulusevski on the right wing. The latter is out injured but Kudus is back in Spurs training. The Ghanian is surely a starter when he is fit.

As a reminder , Bournemouth have made/are continuing to make significant upgrades to the Vitality before their first season in Europe. This was our story back in May after their European qualification was assured.

Bournemouth are facing a race to complete upgrades to the Vitality Stadium to enable it to stage European football next season. Uefa has granted Bournemouth a provisional stadium licence after meeting club officials in April to review their redevelopment project, but improvements are required owing to the limited size of the hospitality areas and broadcasting facilities.

Bournemouth have submitted plans for a phased expansion that would almost double the 11,286 capacity to more than 20,000. Bournemouth do not have to increase their capacity to meet Uefa requirements – Bodø/Glimt competed in the Champions League this season with a stadium holding 8,000 spectators – but infrastructure improvements are needed to gain a Uefa category rating.

“Bournemouth v Milan in the Europa League is a massive clash,” emails Peter Oh. “Of kits, anyway.”

It’s just a shame for Cherries fans that they are at home to the Italian giants in their Europa League opener. Milan will visit the mighty Vitality Stadium (capacity: 12,357) next month.

Sunderland, on the other hand, will go away to San Siro on match-day two of the Europa League, after an opener at home to AZ Alkmaar. What a trip for those Black Cats supporters – I’m desperate to go before the famous old stadium is closed.

Juventus’ talisman, Kenan Yildiz, will undergo an operation on his foot after picking up an injury during Juventus’s opening match of the Serie A season, club affairs officer Giorgio Chiellini said on Friday.

“Kenan is set to undergo surgery and will be out of action for several months,” former Italy international Chiellini told Sky Sport Italia on the sidelines of the Europa League draw. “It’s a serious injury, but it won’t have a lasting impact on his career.”

Yildiz injured his left foot last Sunday during Juve’s 1-0 away win to newly-promoted Frosinone, before being substituted in the 69th minute.

According to the Italian press, the 21-year-old has fractured his fifth metatarsal, which will require surgery expected to take place early next week. He is expected to be sidelined for between two to three months.

Yildiz is regarded by Juve as the undisputed star of their team. He scored 10 goals in 36 league matches last season and took part in the 2026 World Cup, where Turkey were knocked out in the group stage.

Álvaro Arbeloa and Xabi Alonso are former Liverpool, Real Madrid and Spain teammates and remain very close friends. They even have a nickname for each other – Truffles – born from Alonso’s cheeky digs at Arbeloa’s misplaced passes during their time together at Liverpool. “In a training session at Liverpool, we had to give 40-yard passes and every time Xabi landed it on my foot, very measured,” explained Arbeloa in a 2017 documentary entitled Campo de Estrellas. Alonso elaborated: “Then Arbeloa gave a few passes and I was always sent searching for the balls in the trees – with the truffles – and the nickname just stuck.”

Something occurred to me watching Fulham v Chelsea on Monday. The pair are close friends, both new to London. Surely they are socialising together? Perhaps, for example, one will pop over on to the other’s house/hotel to watch Aston Villa v Arsenal on Monday night. Their families presumably know each other well, they are practically neighbours. I wonder how the clubs would feel about any potential ‘socialising’. There is a lot of confidential club information on both sides that they would prefer not to be discussed, especially with the transfer window not closing until Tuesday. I wonder if the clubs have talked to Arbeloa or Alonso about this.

Hello everyone! Ah, yes. The warm bath of club football approaches again.

Let’s get straight into it. There has been a small update to Julián Alvarez situation. Atlético last night doubled down on their position regarding a potential sale to Barcelona – the Argentinian will definitely not be moving from Madrid to Catalonia any time soon . On a side note, I am very intrigued by Alvarez’s facial hair. And not in a good way.

Diego Simeone, normally not someone to be crossed, vowed on Friday welcome Alvarez back into his squad amid the ongoing transfer stalemate. The Atléti manager also confirmed that the 26-year-old won’t be available for Saturday’s trip to Sevilla.

I understand that all the questions will be about Julián. The club has been very clear about what will happen. From a sporting perspective, I hope to help him continue being as important as he still is. My focus is on Sevilla, where he won’t be available. When he returns, we’ll give him everything he needs to feel important. In life, anything can be reversed, as long as we have our health.

With that, I am off. I handover to the very capable hands of Michael who will take up through to Palace v Man City. Enjoy the football.

Ipswich boss Gary O’Neil has no update on Tammy Abraham after it was reported the club wanted to sign the star on loan from Aston Villa.

No, no update as far as I am aware. Sounds like you’re further along with that than I am. Nothing to report on that.

We’re hopefully not finished, we’re still trying to do some business. As to who that is and what positions that will be in, no update from me. We’re still working hard to try and improve the group. My focus now is firmly on the game at the weekend.

The Champions League draw was carried out yesterday with some clubs getting an easier draw than others. But who has the toughest, find out here:

Here is a recap on what Unai Emery had to say about Ollie Watkins and Nicolas Jackson:

We are all in the right condition to play, maybe [Mohammed] Kudus can come on the bench, we have to see. [Micky] Van de Ven is right to play. We have a look, we have to understand at the beginning, or part of the game, like Savio, like Pedro [Porro].

Maybe also at the beginning of the game. [Destiny] Udogie is a good use for us, he’s very important. He played 60 minutes well [against Charlton] as was the plan.

Tottenham had a tough start to the season with a 3-0 loss to Brentford. Maager Roberto de Zerbi has since brought in Omar Marmoush on loan from Manchester City and the boss said of his new player:

A great signing for us, a great player, another great player. Every one of us love him as a player and we hope he can do what he is able to.

I think he can give more solutions in attack, we need players in attack capable to score goals, to play well with the ball also.

He also confirmed Marmoush is available for the club’s game against Newcastle on Saturday.

On the other side of the clash , Brentford boss Keith Andrews has commented on whether his club will have anymore transfer business:

I am not entirely sure. I mentioned it the other day, when the window closes I will be very happy and I meant that. Malick just adds to the quality and competition that we have. Will there be anymore? I am genuinely not sure at the moment. Maybe a couple of loans going out.

The way we work, we were keen to get Malick done but if it didn’t work out, the players [we have], we’re in a really good position to be able to navigate through certainly the first part of the season and into January.

Leeds will play Brentford on Sunday and manager Daniel Farke has confirmed all of his players are available for the clash:

It’s [Ilia] Gruev’s second week training with the team so he’s edging closer and closer. Also some good news was Gudmundsson and Gnonto, as it stands they will join us this afternoon [in training] for the first time after their injuries. We have to wait to see how their body reacts, obviously we just have two days but definitely good news. As it stands, all players are available.

Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris spoke to the media before his team take on Fulham on Sunday and he reacted to their Europa League draw.

He said: “53 years later Sunderland are back in Europe so it’s a bit unknown.

“We can expect strong opponents, different cultures, different experiences and we need that to get better. It’s a huge privilege and we are really proud of this opportunity.”

And on drawing AC Milan: “It’s iconic, Milan. It’s a massive club, massive history so to get back in Europe with that fixture, it’s a symbol.”

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has seemingly confirmed Ollie Watkins’ departure from the club, saying the pair shed tears saying goodbye to one another.

Watkins is rumoured to be joining the Saudi club Al-Hilal but that news has not yet been officially announced.

But before Villa take on Arsenal on Monday, Emery spoke to the media and said:

Watkins said sorry after Brighton. He made a mistake. He always had good behaviour in the club and with me.

He’s a fantastic guy. I told him ‘bye’, with a huge hug and a small cry.

Now it’s a new chapter with Nicolas Jackson. Of course all the best for him in Saudi. We are replacing him.

A recent World Cup winner joins a historically downtrodden club, immediately leads them to their first championship, praises the level of play in the league, speaks fondly of living in the club’s market, extends her contract with the club, leads the club to another championship, is named a league MVP finalist, and breaks the club’s all-time scoring record.

That’s the fairytale of Esther González and Gotham FC – a story that ended abruptly, just nine days after that scoring record was set. On 27 July, Gotham announced that they had mutually parted ways with the striker as she “temporarily steps away from soccer to attend to personal matters in Spain”. The announcement of her departure was full of gushing words going both directions, and was met with understanding and support from the women’s soccer world.

New managers are facing an almost one-in-two chance of being fired before the end of the season, a finding from Guardian analysis that shows 22 of the last 50 permanent Premier League managers to leave their roles lasted less than a year.

The betting markets reflect this reality. Six of the eight Premier League managers deemed most likely by bookmakers to be next to leave their post were appointed in 2026. Football management is a very precarious employment position. It looks inevitable that some of the 11 men who have only been in their role since earlier this year will fall before the final hurdle of the 2026-27 season – even if none of them are the first to move on.

We will hear from more managers this afternoon but let’s check in with some stories you may have missed.

Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also been chatting to the media before his team take on Brighton on Sunday. Here are some highlights:

On Enzo Fernandez potentially leaving the club: “We have been talking about speculation, sorry, but I’m not the one who talks too early. We will see what happens. We want to be ready always.”

On how his squad is shaping up as the transfer window heads for its conclusion: “I think overall the balance of what we have is going to be good. We have to see how the last few days develop. But so far the team is coming together. It is a process that will take time. We are in a good position, with a few more days to see.”

On balancing a big squad: “It’s important to respect and know that not all the players are in the same stage of their career. Some players are established, some players it is their first year at a club like Chelsea or even in the Premier League. Everything is at a different stage. They understand that and know that, which is all in the creation of the team. I don’t have a number, I have an idea. We will be close to that.”

United will play Ipswich Town this Sunday but they will be without Amad Diallo and latest signing Carlos Baleba.

Manager Michael Carrick said Baleba will be out for a few weeks with an ankle problem.

“But we knew that before, so it’s no major issue,” Carrick added. “It’ll be great to have him back when we can.

“We’re delighted with Carlos. I think he has huge potential. It’s a really exciting signing for us. I think the quality that he has, the attributes that he has, they balance [the rest of] the group. Different strengths, different combinations. With the player that he already is, with that little bit more to come from him, this is exciting for us.”

James Ward-Prowse has signed for his former club Southampton on a two-year deal from West Ham.

The England international initially left in 2023 after 410 appearances for the club, who now compete in the Championship.

Ward-Prowse said: “It feels a bit surreal. The last couple of days have been pretty intense, but I’m delighted to be back, and to be wearing the red and white again is truly special.

“It’s the place I call home, obviously having come through the Academy since I was eight. It was an incredible journey up until the point that I left, but home is a special place and I always had it in the back of my mind that it was somewhere that I wanted to be. I’m here today very excited and looking forward to the challenge ahead.”

Senegal international El Hadji Malick Diouf has joined Brentford from West Ham for around £40m. The 21-year-old defender has signed a five-year deal at the Gtech Community Stadium with the option of another season. “He’s a player that fits our ideal age profile, with lots of room to still develop,” said Bees boss Keith Andrews.

“He had a really good year at West Ham in his first season in English football, and some of the qualities and attributes he has as a full-back really add to an already impressive part of our team.” PA Media

Celtic and Rangers have both been ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup match behind closed doors. The punishment comes following a Scottish FA disciplinary hearing into the trouble that marred Celtic’s quarter-final win at Ibrox in March. Dozens of arrests were made following clashes on the pitch after Rangers fans charged on to confront Celtic supporters who had spilled on to the playing area to celebrate their team’s penalty shoot-out success.

Both clubs will have to pay their opponents £100,000 in compensation for the loss of shared gate receipts at the cup ties. Any repeat of crowd trouble at Scottish Cup ties in the next two seasons would prompt another closed-door punishment. Both clubs admitted charges relating to unacceptable conduct from supporters. An independent review into the scenes previously concluded that “crushing” and “life-threatening violence” were narrowly avoided. PA Media
paragraphs: That’s all we have time for on this blog . Thank you for reading and for your emails. I’ll leave you with The Talk, a handy round-up of some of the best Friday newslines
Oh, and I am now helming our minute-by-minute report of today’s Premier League clash: Crystal Palace v Manchester City (8pm BST kick-off). Join me!

Not a sentence I thought I would be typing today : Álvaro Morata has joined Spanish second-division side Leganés, on loan from Italian side Como! The veteran striker, 33, Morata played 26 matches in Serie A last season as Como qualified for the Champions League, a competition he won twice with Real Madrid.
Leganés said on their website they would have “an option to buy [Morata] at the end of the season”.

It is not the fixture that Derek McInnes would have wanted following Rangers’ disastrous penalty-shootout defeat in their Conference League qualifier at Jablonec in the Czech Republic, but the Glasgow side head to Pittodrie for a tough away day at Aberdeen on Sunday. The Ibrox club had earlier been eliminated from the Europa League by Jagiellonia Bialystok and Rangers have won just two of their seven games this season under McInnes.
Lawrence Shankland, the newly-appointed captain following his summer move from Hearts, has said this of Rangers’ European heartache:

There’s been plenty of low moments in football, but this is certainly one that’s right up there in terms of how bad it feels. This is a real tough blow but we need to stick together, we need to find it in ourselves to have that togetherness and that’s hard at times like this, because you can tend to go on as an individual and look after number one and we can’t have that in the difficult times. We need to try and stick together as a team and rally around each other. Over two legs it wasn’t good enough.

We’ll need to go and watch it back, but there were times in the second half that they were causing us a lot of problems and we just didn’t get to grips with the game at all. In terms of moments, it probably felt like they were the team that were going to have one and we never did done enough at the top end to create a clear-cut chance or have that moment, and that’s disappointing.

Cole Palmer is genuinely unusual in the modern game . He turns up in strange spaces, finds gullies and currents in between those static pegs. Right now he is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there, in the sense of inventing the game in front of him, dishing up in those moments the pure pleasure of a story being told in real time.

He even looks a little unusual in an era of hyper-athletes. Palmer is light and mobile. He can turn with balletic grace. But he also has that gangly, mischievous physicality, like a very clever cartoon alpaca has worked out how to put on a royal blue football kit and run around occasionally doing amusing celebrations.
Brighton have confirmed the appointment of Arturo Ruiz from Real Sociedad as a replacement head coach for Dario Vidosic.

The Women’s Super League club have acted quickly to replace Vidosic, whose departure was confirmed earlier on Friday, just over a week before the start of the new Women’s Super League campaign. Vidosic is understood to be the leading candidate for the head coach role at the NWSL side Angel City and although Brighton are disappointed to lose the Croatia-born Australian, they are understood to be very happy to be able to bring in Ruiz on a three-year deal, subject to a work permit being finalised.

More bad news for Crystal Palace after the London side lost Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea and Chadi Riad during last weekend’s 2-0 defeat at Everton. Now a deal for Club Brugge defender Joel Ordóñez, could be called off after reported complications with the centre-back’s medical.
Palace looked like they had beaten Aston Villa to the signing of Ordóñez, who is recovering from a broken metatarsal. But it looks like the injury is worse than it was initially thought to be.

Manchester United have signed the Sweden winger Monica Jusu Bah from the Swedish side BK Häcken on a deal until June 2030, for an undisclosed fee reportedly in excess of £400,000. The 23-year-old helped Häcken lift last season’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup. She told Manchester United’s website: “It’s an unbelievable feeling to join Manchester United. There is a real togetherness in the group, and you can feel the excitement from everyone, for a big season ahead. “The opportunity to work with Eva Olid is perfect, everybody knows the quality of her coaching and her ability to support players to reach their highest level. I’m ready to keep pushing myself, help the team achieve our ambitions together and create special memories at this incredible club.”
That is a name I haven’t heard in a while. Was part of that famous Valencia side and good on Championship Manager, if I remember correctly.

González, 52, has ⁠a close relationship with ​Lionel ​Messi, which I imagine is a huge reason for his appointment. He previously has served ​as the head coach ​at ‌Argentine sides ​Rosario ​Central, Union (Santa Fe) and Platense.
A bit more from Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi, who wants one more signing despite Spurs already spending around £300m this summer.

I didn’t expect a market like we have done,” De Zerbi said. “I think we can do one player more and in one specific position. Yesterday we went for dinner with the owner, with Vinai [Venkatesham, the chief executive], with Johan [Lange, the sporting director] and with Enrico [Venturelli, De Zerbi’s assistant]. We spoke about this but we have all of us on the same page and there is a very good connection.

It can be possible out or in. The transfer market is crazy and we have to be able to find the new players. If some players go out, leave, or to make another player [come] in … I don’t know. We are very happy with the market we have done until now. It has been more than my expectation at the beginning.”

I understand why Tottenham spent money on Omar Marmoush – Richarlison and Dominic Solanke are not reliable for form and fitness – but I can’t really get my head around Spurs spent £75m on Savinho/Sávio , given they already have Mohammed Kudus and Deki Kulusevski on the right wing. The latter is out injured but Kudus is back in Spurs training. The Ghanian is surely a starter when he is fit.

Tottenham had a tough start to the season with a 3-0 loss to Brentford. Maager Roberto de Zerbi has since brought in Omar Marmoush on loan from Manchester City and the boss said of his new player:
A great signing for us, a great player, another great player. Every one of us love him as a player and we hope he can do what he is able to.
I think he can give more solutions in attack, we need players in attack capable to score goals, to play well with the ball also.
He also confirmed Marmoush is available for the club’s game against Newcastle on Saturday.
On the other side of the clash , Brentford boss Keith Andrews has commented on whether his club will have anymore transfer business:

I am not entirely sure. I mentioned it the other day, when the window closes I will be very happy and I meant that. Malick just adds to the quality and competition that we have. Will there be anymore? I am genuinely not sure at the moment. Maybe a couple of loans going out.

The way we work, we were keen to get Malick done but if it didn’t work out, the players [we have], we’re in a really good position to be able to navigate through certainly the first part of the season and into January.
Leeds will play Brentford on Sunday and manager Daniel Farke has confirmed all of his players are available for the clash:

It’s [Ilia] Gruev’s second week training with the team so he’s edging closer and closer. Also some good news was Gudmundsson and Gnonto, as it stands they will join us this afternoon [in training] for the first time after their injuries. We have to wait to see how their body reacts, obviously we just have two days but definitely good news. As it stands, all players are available.
Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris spoke to the media before his team take on Fulham on Sunday and he reacted to their Europa League draw.
He said: “53 years later Sunderland are back in Europe so it’s a bit unknown.
“We can expect strong opponents, different cultures, different experiences and we need that to get better. It’s a huge privilege and we are really proud of this opportunity.”
And on drawing AC Milan: “It’s iconic, Milan. It’s a massive club, massive history so to get back in Europe with that fixture, it’s a symbol.”
Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has seemingly confirmed Ollie Watkins’ departure from the club, saying the pair shed tears saying goodbye to one another.
Watkins is rumoured to be joining the Saudi club Al-Hilal but that news has not yet been officially announced.
But before Villa take on Arsenal on Monday, Emery spoke to the media and said:
Watkins said sorry after Brighton. He made a mistake. He always had good behaviour in the club and with me.
He’s a fantastic guy. I told him ‘bye’, with a huge hug and a small cry.
Now it’s a new chapter with Nicolas Jackson. Of course all the best for him in Saudi. We are replacing him.

A recent World Cup winner joins a historically downtrodden club, immediately leads them to their first championship, praises the level of play in the league, speaks fondly of living in the club’s market, extends her contract with the club, leads the club to another championship, is named a league MVP finalist, and breaks the club’s all-time scoring record.

That’s the fairytale of Esther González and Gotham FC – a story that ended abruptly, just nine days after that scoring record was set. On 27 July, Gotham announced that they had mutually parted ways with the striker as she “temporarily steps away from soccer to attend to personal matters in Spain”. The announcement of her departure was full of gushing words going both directions, and was met with understanding and support from the women’s soccer world.

New managers are facing an almost one-in-two chance of being fired before the end of the season, a finding from Guardian analysis that shows 22 of the last 50 permanent Premier League managers to leave their roles lasted less than a year.

The betting markets reflect this reality. Six of the eight Premier League managers deemed most likely by bookmakers to be next to leave their post were appointed in 2026. Football management is a very precarious employment position. It looks inevitable that some of the 11 men who have only been in their role since earlier this year will fall before the final hurdle of the 2026-27 season – even if none of them are the first to move on.
We will hear from more managers this afternoon but let’s check in with some stories you may have missed.
Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also been chatting to the media before his team take on Brighton on Sunday. Here are some highlights:
On Enzo Fernandez potentially leaving the club: “We have been talking about speculation, sorry, but I’m not the one who talks too early. We will see what happens. We want to be ready always.”

On how his squad is shaping up as the transfer window heads for its conclusion: “I think overall the balance of what we have is going to be good. We have to see how the last few days develop. But so far the team is coming together. It is a process that will take time. We are in a good position, with a few more days to see.”

On balancing a big squad: “It’s important to respect and know that not all the players are in the same stage of their career. Some players are established, some players it is their first year at a club like Chelsea or even in the Premier League. Everything is at a different stage. They understand that and know that, which is all in the creation of the team. I don’t have a number, I have an idea. We will be close to that.”
United will play Ipswich Town this Sunday but they will be without Amad Diallo and latest signing Carlos Baleba.
Manager Michael Carrick said Baleba will be out for a few weeks with an ankle problem.
“But we knew that before, so it’s no major issue,” Carrick added. “It’ll be great to have him back when we can.

“We’re delighted with Carlos. I think he has huge potential. It’s a really exciting signing for us. I think the quality that he has, the attributes that he has, they balance [the rest of] the group. Different strengths, different combinations. With the player that he already is, with that little bit more to come from him, this is exciting for us.”
James Ward-Prowse has signed for his former club Southampton on a two-year deal from West Ham.
The England international initially left in 2023 after 410 appearances for the club, who now compete in the Championship.
Ward-Prowse said: “It feels a bit surreal. The last couple of days have been pretty intense, but I’m delighted to be back, and to be wearing the red and white again is truly special.

“It’s the place I call home, obviously having come through the Academy since I was eight. It was an incredible journey up until the point that I left, but home is a special place and I always had it in the back of my mind that it was somewhere that I wanted to be. I’m here today very excited and looking forward to the challenge ahead.”

Senegal international El Hadji Malick Diouf has joined Brentford from West Ham for around £40m. The 21-year-old defender has signed a five-year deal at the Gtech Community Stadium with the option of another season. “He’s a player that fits our ideal age profile, with lots of room to still develop,” said Bees boss Keith Andrews.

“He had a really good year at West Ham in his first season in English football, and some of the qualities and attributes he has as a full-back really add to an already impressive part of our team.” PA Media
