Celtic and Rangers have both been ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup match behind closed doors. The punishment comes following a Scottish FA disciplinary hearing into the trouble that marred Celtic’s quarter-final win at Ibrox in March. Dozens of arrests were made following clashes on the pitch after Rangers fans charged on to confront Celtic supporters who had spilled on to the playing area to celebrate their team’s penalty shoot-out success.

Both clubs will have to pay their opponents £100,000 in compensation for the loss of shared gate receipts at the cup ties. Any repeat of crowd trouble at Scottish Cup ties in the next two seasons would prompt another closed-door punishment. Both clubs admitted charges relating to unacceptable conduct from supporters. An independent review into the scenes previously concluded that “crushing” and “life-threatening violence” were narrowly avoided. PA Media

articles.title: Gatwick Airport faced water outage after main burst
articles.summary: SES Water says it has repaired a burst main which was affecting supply to the airport.
articles.content:
Gatwick Airport has been hit with a water outage after a burst main in Horley, SES Water says

Gatwick Airport passengers were left without water after a main burst in a nearby field.

SES Water said that it located a burst main in Horley, with parts of the airport left without water as a result.

A spokesperson for the airport confirmed that the issue had affected water supply in both terminals and was under investigation by SES Water. The water company said it had begun to restore supply and that water pressure was beginning to return to normal.

The issues come after a major supply outage in July saw passengers face long queues for toilets at the West Sussex airport, with restaurants and bars also closing.

Natasha Nzekwe, who was due to fly to Amsterdam from the North Terminal, said: "It's quite frustrating, but everyone seems to be pretty fine.

"There's no water at all, you can't even wash your hands in the toilets.

"If I were on a long haul flight I think it would be worse, not being able to properly wash your hands is frustrating, and they haven't given us any information as to what is going on."

Naduni Abeywickrama, who was travelling from London to Aberdeen, added that the delay was "extremely frustrating".

She added: "No one seems to be making a scene, but I feel frustrated because this is the second time this has happened."

Toilets in the airport's North Terminal are closed as a result of the supply issue, while the majority of toilets in the South Terminal are unaffected.

Food outlets in the North Terminal remain open, but for passenger seating only.

Anthony Rochester, head of networks at SES Water, said that it "had restored water supplies to Gatwick Airport and the surrounding areas by re-routing our network".

"We're continuing to work closely with the airport as we understand water isn't yet flowing throughout their buildings", he added.

A Gatwick Airport spokesperson said: "Toilets have remained available throughout, and food and beverage outlets are now reopening and serving hot food.

"Since becoming aware of the issue, we have been working closely with our airport partners to help minimise the impact and successfully ensure all of today's flights continue to depart as scheduled.

"We recognise the inconvenience caused by today's water shortage and thank passengers for their patience and understanding. We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

In July, both terminals at Gatwick Airport lost running water for several hours after a power failure at a treatment works in the area.

articles.title: Premier League news: ‘Mackems in Milan’ as Le Bris revels in Sunderland’s rise
articles.summary: Sunderland will visit San Siro in Europa League while Carlos Baleba must wait for his Manchester United debut Continue reading...
articles.content:
Sunderland will visit San Siro in Europa League while Carlos Baleba must wait for his Manchester United debut

Regis Le Bris has said Sunderland’s forthcoming trip to Milan in the Europa League is “a symbol” of the club’s upward trajectory. For many years Newcastle fans have taunted their local rivals with chants of “You’ll never see a Mackem in Milan” and, after arriving from Brittany two years ago, Le Bris swiftly learned that St James’ Park regulars regarded themselves as distinctly superior to Sunderland supporters.

Now, though, the tables have turned and Le Bris is enjoying the moment. Sunderland’s manager agreed that it seemed somehow appropriate that the first fixture involving his team to be drawn in Monaco on Friday featured a trip to San Siro.

“To get back in Europe with this fixture, it’s a symbol,” said Le Bris, whose side finished seventh in the Premier League last season after beating Newcastle home and away. “It’s iconic. Milan is a massive club and it’s a massive story.

“I’m aware of it [the Newcastle fans’ Milan jibes], but I want to speak more about us. We are proud to be in Sunderland and our fans deserve to be in this position. It’s [going to be] a huge experience and we are very proud to be part of it but we want to be efficient. We want to be competitive in the Europa League.”

As Sunderland fans began ordering T-shirts and sweatshirts emblazoned with the message “Mackem in Milan” to wear in northern Italy, Le Bris seemed delighted that three players, goalkeeper Robin Roefs, winger Romaine Mundle and the forward Wilson Isidor have signed new long term contracts at the Stadium of Light.

“They see their future in Sunderland because they trust the club and like the environment and they trust the ambition of the club,” said a manager whose side will also face AZ, Dinamo Zagreb, Levski Sofia and Jagiellonia at the Stadium of Light and Anderlecht, Lech Poznan and Torreense away in the Europa League.

Le Bris, whose team are at home to Fulham on Sunday, declined to comment on Sunderland’s attempt to sign Jack Grealish on loan from Manchester City but it is believed the former England winger is now most likely to re-join Everton.

Sunderland, meanwhile, remain in the hunt for a right winger and a striker this summer. “I trust the recruitment staff,” said Le Bris. “We are well aligned about the targets we need to make the team better and I still think that we will succeed in the transfer market.” Louise Taylor

Matthias Jaissle is convinced new arrival Nico González will not take long to hit the ground running following his big-money arrival from Manchester City. The Spaniard could make his Newcastle debut on Saturday at Tottenham following a move from City that could rise to £52m this week, with the head coach excited by the 24-year-old’s ceiling.

“He trained with us and he looks sharp,” Jaissle said. “It will take time [to adapt] and I can not tell you how long it takes but he’s a smart player, he has huge potential and already brings so much quality in the squad. He will adapt fast into our way of playing and then we can enjoy.”

Jaissle is hopeful that Gonzalez will not be the last player through the door at St James’ Park in this summer’s window, with the Belgium wideman Matias Fernandez-Pardo tipped to move to Tyneside from Lille. “It’s the first message of the morning – to push,” Jaissle said. “The management and Ross [Wilson], the sporting director, they’re doing an amazing job, trying everything. “We want to be smart, we don’t want to act in panic, so I’m really optimistic things will happen.” PA Media

Oliver Glasner expects more signings at Nottingham Forest following the arrival of the striker Liam Delap. The 23-year-old joined from Chelsea for a club-record £45m fee on Thursday, and Glasner plans to make further additions before Tuesday’s transfer deadline.

Glasner would not comment on a reported £22m Forest offer for his former Crystal Palace wing-back Daniel Munoz, but the Austrian did admit prospective deals were close to completion. “I think we will add two players,” Glasner said before Saturday’s trip to Liverpool and on the back of home league and Carabao Cup defeats to Leeds.

“One we have added, that means we will have at least one more signing. Close deals, quite close to be done, but now from today our focus is on the Liverpool match. That is the most important thing in the next 30 hours and then we have three more days to get the deals over the line.”

Delap left Chelsea after scoring only two goals in all competitions following his move from Ipswich last summer, and was made to train away from the first-team squad by new Blues manager Xabi Alonso. Glasner said: “It is clear you have to look for a club where you have better chances to get minutes and reignite your career, and that is why we think we are the right club for him.” PA Media

Gary O’Neil has insisted Ipswich are not finished in the transfer window after another busy week at the Premier League newcomers. Argentina international and World Cup winner Exequiel Palacios arrived at Portman Road on Thursday in the latest big-money move secured by the Suffolk club.

Talks remain ongoing with the Aston Vila forward Tammy Abraham, who is yet to make a decision on whether to join on a season-long loan, it is understood, but O’Neil is hopeful more can occur in the coming days.

Before Sunday’s trip to Manchester United, O’Neil told a press conference: “No, nothing to report on that [Abraham move]. We’re hopefully not finished. We’re still trying to do some business. As to who that is or what positions that will be in, there’s no update from me.

“We’re still working hard to try and improve the group, but my focus now is firmly on the game at the weekend and making sure that we’re fully prepared for what is going to be an incredibly tough test.”

Ipswich could have Florentino Luis involved at Old Trafford and Palacios is set to make his debut. Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor remain sidelined. PA Media

Michael Carrick has confirmed “really exciting” addition Carlos Baleba will be unable to make his Manchester United debut for around three weeks due to an ankle injury.

Following the summer arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, United further bolstered their midfield by completing the £70m signing of the 22-year-old from Brighton on Tuesday. United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, hailed Baleba as “an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further” but fans will have to wait to see him play for the club.

The Cameroon international arrived at Old Trafford with an ankle injury, which Carrick says will rule him out of Sunday’s Premier League home opener against promoted Ipswich and beyond. “He’s got a little ankle issue, so maybe a couple of weeks or so, maybe three weeks,” Carrick said. “We’ll see but we knew that before, so it’s no major issue but it’ll be great to have him back when we can.”

Asked if Baleba and Amad Diallo, another injured player, could return before the new three-week international break, the United manager said: “It’s obviously new, the break to deal with, but we’ll wait and see. We’re hopeful but I don’t want to put any deadlines on it just yet. Amad won’t be involved this week. He’ll be out for a little bit longer. Mase [Mason Mount] is back around the group, which was great. Trained this week, so that’s a big positive for us.” PA Media

Sunderland, meanwhile, remain in the hunt for a right winger and a striker this summer. “I trust the recruitment staff,” said Le Bris. “We are well aligned about the targets we need to make the team better and I still think that we will succeed in the transfer market.” Louise Taylor

Matthias Jaissle is convinced new arrival Nico González will not take long to hit the ground running following his big-money arrival from Manchester City. The Spaniard could make his Newcastle debut on Saturday at Tottenham following a move from City that could rise to £52m this week, with the head coach excited by the 24-year-old’s ceiling.

“He trained with us and he looks sharp,” Jaissle said. “It will take time [to adapt] and I can not tell you how long it takes but he’s a smart player, he has huge potential and already brings so much quality in the squad. He will adapt fast into our way of playing and then we can enjoy.”

Jaissle is hopeful that Gonzalez will not be the last player through the door at St James’ Park in this summer’s window, with the Belgium wideman Matias Fernandez-Pardo tipped to move to Tyneside from Lille. “It’s the first message of the morning – to push,” Jaissle said. “The management and Ross [Wilson], the sporting director, they’re doing an amazing job, trying everything. “We want to be smart, we don’t want to act in panic, so I’m really optimistic things will happen.” PA Media

Oliver Glasner expects more signings at Nottingham Forest following the arrival of the striker Liam Delap. The 23-year-old joined from Chelsea for a club-record £45m fee on Thursday, and Glasner plans to make further additions before Tuesday’s transfer deadline.

Glasner would not comment on a reported £22m Forest offer for his former Crystal Palace wing-back Daniel Munoz, but the Austrian did admit prospective deals were close to completion. “I think we will add two players,” Glasner said before Saturday’s trip to Liverpool and on the back of home league and Carabao Cup defeats to Leeds.

“One we have added, that means we will have at least one more signing. Close deals, quite close to be done, but now from today our focus is on the Liverpool match. That is the most important thing in the next 30 hours and then we have three more days to get the deals over the line.”

Delap left Chelsea after scoring only two goals in all competitions following his move from Ipswich last summer, and was made to train away from the first-team squad by new Blues manager Xabi Alonso. Glasner said: “It is clear you have to look for a club where you have better chances to get minutes and reignite your career, and that is why we think we are the right club for him.” PA Media

Gary O’Neil has insisted Ipswich are not finished in the transfer window after another busy week at the Premier League newcomers. Argentina international and World Cup winner Exequiel Palacios arrived at Portman Road on Thursday in the latest big-money move secured by the Suffolk club.

Talks remain ongoing with the Aston Vila forward Tammy Abraham, who is yet to make a decision on whether to join on a season-long loan, it is understood, but O’Neil is hopeful more can occur in the coming days.

“We’re still working hard to try and improve the group, but my focus now is firmly on the game at the weekend and making sure that we’re fully prepared for what is going to be an incredibly tough test.”

Following the summer arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, United further bolstered their midfield by completing the £70m signing of the 22-year-old from Brighton on Tuesday. United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, hailed Baleba as “an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further” but fans will have to wait to see him play for the club.

The Cameroon international arrived at Old Trafford with an ankle injury, which Carrick says will rule him out of Sunday’s Premier League home opener against promoted Ipswich and beyond. “He’s got a little ankle issue, so maybe a couple of weeks or so, maybe three weeks,” Carrick said. “We’ll see but we knew that before, so it’s no major issue but it’ll be great to have him back when we can.”

Asked if Baleba and Amad Diallo, another injured player, could return before the new three-week international break, the United manager said: “It’s obviously new, the break to deal with, but we’ll wait and see. We’re hopeful but I don’t want to put any deadlines on it just yet. Amad won’t be involved this week. He’ll be out for a little bit longer. Mase [Mason Mount] is back around the group, which was great. Trained this week, so that’s a big positive for us.” PA Media

articles.content:
Much like Central Cee, the Chelsea attacker is a distinct presence and right now is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there

T his week Central Cee launched his new Premier League song, called The Team. It owes its existence to a youth-centred, fist-bumping corporate tie-in with Coca-Cola, the press release for which appears to have involved a man in golf-casual clothing frowning at his computer screen for half an hour before typing “cool urban street words, what are?” into the AI search box, then nipping off for a quick brain-bowl strategy lunch with Roger from the Bluesky Synergy hub.

The song is really good, because Central Cee is really good. He’s super-smart with words, funny and snappy, but also surprisingly tender and raw.

And yes, this is an oh-no-dad’s-talking-about-rap moment. You can just scroll down if you like. The whole thing moves on to Cole Palmer very quickly, why he’s both the best English footballer and very easy to love currently, for various reasons.

Central Cee is a significant figure, perhaps the biggest British recording artist right now. He’s also oddly raw and fearless in the things he says, in a way that feels distinct from the standard, mannered modern person, and which has got him into trouble at least once.

A few years back there was a furore when Central Cee decided to speak out against sexual prejudice. This sounds as if it should just be fine. Except, Central Cee’s call for tolerance was expressed via a lyric in the song Doja. And that lyric was: “How can I be homophobic? My bitch is gay.”

Hmm. Problems there. What Central Cee is saying here, what Central Cee has done while appearing to express a progressive sensibility, is to introduce an entirely new tier of … Basically what he’s saying is: how can I be homophobic? I’m far too busy being sexist.

This caused understandable offence. The b-word is demeaning and cheap, whatever your intentions. Don’t say it. Find better words. To his credit, Central Cee was very good at explaining and apologising, open to other views, while also seeming genuinely non-judgmental of other people regardless of difference or identity, with the exception, of course, of wastemen, mugs and snitches.

He seems to have been forgiven now. More than that, he’s startlingly successful, the most streamed British rap artist of all time. Young people respond to him hungrily. He seems adaptive, fitted to the modern world. In the Coke video he looks blankly into the lens, gives you everything and nothing, risky but also weirdly fearless.

What does this have to do with Cole Palmer, and the surge of heartfelt Palmer-love across all platforms this week after his brilliant performance against Fulham on Monday?

First, Palmer is good friends with Central Cee. He even turned up at the launch of the Coke song just before Chelsea’s Premier League opener. And Palmer really was sensational at Craven Cottage, twirling about between the defensive lines, all perfect touch and interesting angles.

The reaction was significant too. Everyone went wild for this. In particular passionate football men of a certain age went wild. This boy is gold, this boy gets people off their seats, the man in the TalkSport video chair growled, speaking from the gut and the spleen, coming off less like a piece of football analysis, more like a man offering a brave, husky funeral elegy for a very loyal family dog.

This passion does have an edge to it. It is a mark of how hungry we are for something different, a counterpoint to the dominance of systems football, that despite being entirely academy-coded Palmer still seems to be a unicorn in this world.

For the middle-aged proper football man he can look like a flicker of the pre-digital memory, football in the time of maverick authenticity, an age of mud, of landlines, of not wearing a seat belt, of smoking in pubs, of the casually discarded woodland porn mag, of Barry Davies shouting: “Oh, it’s magnificent and can’t they just taste it” while mods throw darts at each other in the background, because old fun is the best fun.

This is, of course, both deluded and incorrect, because football encourages such feelings and because many middle-aged men are already both of these things. But Palmer is genuinely unusual in the modern game. He turns up in strange spaces, finds gullies and currents in between those static pegs.

Right now he is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there, in the sense of inventing the game in front of him, dishing up in those moments the pure pleasure of a story being told in real time.

He even looks a little unusual in an era of hyper‑athletes. Palmer is light and mobile. He can turn with balletic grace. But he also has that gangly, mischievous physicality, like a very clever cartoon alpaca has worked out how to put on a royal blue football kit and run around occasionally doing amusing celebrations.

From here Palmer will benefit from having a very good club manager who gets his position. At Bayer Leverkusen Xabi Alonso designed an entire team around getting the best out of Florian Wirtz, the “free electron” in the structure.

Beyond this, Palmer is clearly the player the national team should have been configured around after Euro 2024. It made some logical sense not to pick him for the World Cup, because merit and fitness are also important. But Thomas Tuchel simply has to play Palmer, Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane together now, even if you have to pack the team with cement sacks and tins of beans to make it work, because this is just incredibly hot, and there is literally no other point in playing these games.

But it isn’t just the football. Palmer is also just weirdly likable. There is a temptation to cast him as a Lego-haired blank, some kind of urban idiot savant, a human being made entirely from white bread, energy drinks and discarded phone cases. But he’s clearly very smart, and also very modern in his own way.

This is another element of the Palmer persona. He looks unbothered, wry and oddly gentle. But the blankness is a thing, a way of being in the middle of all that glare. Palmer gives you nothing to bite on, no gaps in the armour. He even seems weirdly post-race, or just non-race, some kind of bowl-headed omni-man.

It is both an attitude and a shield of sorts. There’s a thing young people do on the internet, known as Nonchalance. This is all about projecting indifference and impassive facial expressions, appearing comically unbothered while chaotic things happen around you. In the picture with Central Cee at the Coke thing they’re both doing it, staring blankly into the camera open but also closed.

Palmer seems to do this naturally. He will sit with his legs crossed while a group of angry men have an on-pitch brawl nearby. He will have the sense of raw dramatic irony to look genuinely amused on the live TV feed as the referee stands right in the middle of the Chelsea huddle , one of the most comically weird sub-moments of the modern age.

There is a theory nonchalance is a political attitude, a response by the post-Gen-Z demographic to the challenge of making the world you find less incoherent, less intrusive on your space, a blank against the constant wall of noise, dogma and ideological boilerplate hurled your way.

Even the way Palmer plays has a kind of shrug about it, an existential creativity, making up your own patterns, making the world small, you-sized, following the lines in front of you.

One of the best bits of Monday night’s game was his interview after. Sky’s reporter Emma Saunders asked Palmer: “How ready are you for this season?” His response was: “Did you not watch the game?” – which from some old‑school, spam-faced football man might have sounded a bit weird, a bit off on power dynamic, a bit man-woman.

But it really wasn’t that at all. Palmer was already laughing. Saunders laughed back. And it was just a nice moment, banter-stuff, mate-chat, playing the game in front of you. English football has such an interesting figure here, not just a brilliant footballer, but a distinct presence, a way of existing in the middle of all that heat. Let’s try not to break him this time.

articles.title: Infallible style: Pope Leo appears in Vanity Fair’s ranks of most fashionable

Featuring 70 names, the list ranks the most fashionable people in the world in 2026. The lineup includes the usual suspects spanning Hollywood actors and global pop stars but nestled among the Hollywood stars is an unexpected entrant. Pope Leo XIV. A simple white cassock styled with a pair of Nike trainers. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Pontiff, who has caught the eye in trainers and a baseball cap, praised for taking dress to ‘heavenly heights’

For the first time in a decade, Vanity Fair has released a best-dressed list . Featuring 70 names, the list ranks the most fashionable people in the world in 2026. The lineup includes the usual suspects spanning Hollywood actors and global pop stars but nestled among the Hollywood stars is an unexpected entrant. Pope Leo XIV.

The 70-year-old head of the Catholic church has been praised by the magazine for taking papal style “to heavenly heights”. His most memorable look? A simple white cassock styled with a pair of Nike trainers.

Vanity Fair’s style correspondent José Criales-Unzueta, who worked on compiling the list, said he and the team were impressed by the “innate Americanness” of the way the pope dressed.

The Chicago-born pontiff has carved out a style niche and garnered a loyal fashion following with his enthusiasm for both bespoke vestments and vintage fashion accessories. Alongside trainers, he prefers simple black oxford shoes to the traditional red papal slippers.

He wears a discontinued Swiss-made quartz watch, carries his own battered briefcase and in June 2025 popped a White Sox baseball cap over his papal cap for a general audience in St Peter’s Square. For more formal occasions, he turns to the Italian designer Filippo Sorcinelli, who also created liturgical vestments for the previous popes Benedict XVI and Francis.

The Catholic church, with its long mastery of symbolism and optics, is experiencing an uptick driven by gen Z. For Leo, being featured in a publication that its global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, has described as a “magazine about personalities” and that feels “like the pantheon” works well with the papacy’s own aim to position itself as a modern power.

“The world’s embrace of this pope has been stunning to me,” said Robert Orsi, a professor of religious studies at Northwestern University in Illinois. Orsi pointed to Leo’s criticism of AI and calls for peace as also speaking to gen Z.

Carol Richardson, a professor of early modern art history at the University of Edinburgh, said the pope, who has his own Instagram account, would be aware of his inclusion on the list. “He and the people surrounding him are very savvy,” she said. “The majority will think it’s fun. They will like the fact it has been noticed how busy he is, that he has to wear trainers to run around in. That he is working.”

From Christian Lacroix ecclesiastical riffing in the 80s and the Met’s Heavenly Bodies exhibition in 2018 to crucifixes and depictions of Christ on the most recent catwalks, the papacy has long fascinated fashion. Criales-Unzueta says its appeal lies in its vastness. “There is so much to take in and so much to find inspiration in.”

The pontiff is listed in Vanity Fair’s “originals” division, a category of individuals commended by the magazine for being “the most outlandish and innovative dressers” with “a singular point of view”. Others on the list include the film-maker Spike Lee and the singers Björk and Rosalía.

Criales-Unzueta described the list as “an opportunity to showcase the way fashion and style are deeply embedded in culture and society” and that “style, good style, is a practice that is not reserved for celebrities or their stylists”.

When Leo was first spotted last May wearing Nike trainers in a still from Leone a Roma, a Vatican-produced documentary that retraces his time in Rome before he became pope, the image instantly went viral. Many people mistook it as fake. It was compared to the AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing an oversized Balenciaga puffer jacket, which has since been described as “the first real mass-level AI misinformation case” . Criales-Unzueta said that was the moment Leo became “a talking point in and outside of fashion”. Trainer fans were quick to identify Leo’s Nikes as a discontinued retro tennis-style shoe that was first sold in the 70s. “What a papal flex,” declared Esquire , while some online users were quick to christen his style as “holy drip”.

By the end of last year, Leo found himself featured alongside A$AP Rocky and Bad Bunny in Vogue’s best-dressed list, while the New York Times named him as one of its 67 Most Stylish People of 2025.

Orsi said he had been thinking about what the trainers symbolised. “A sportiness? A familiarity with track and field, basketball courts, running?” he pondered. For him it was “a lightness on his feet, a readiness to move quickly to where he is needed the most”, he said. “They signal that he is approachable, like a good coach, and also humble.”

The pontiff is listed in Vanity Fair’s “originals” division, a category of individuals commended by the magazine for being “the most outlandish and innovative dressers” with “a singular point of view”. Others on the list include the film-maker Spike Lee and the singers Björk and Rosalía.

Criales-Unzueta described the list as “an opportunity to showcase the way fashion and style are deeply embedded in culture and society” and that “style, good style, is a practice that is not reserved for celebrities or their stylists”.

When Leo was first spotted last May wearing Nike trainers in a still from Leone a Roma, a Vatican-produced documentary that retraces his time in Rome before he became pope, the image instantly went viral. Many people mistook it as fake. It was compared to the AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing an oversized Balenciaga puffer jacket, which has since been described as “the first real mass-level AI misinformation case” . Criales-Unzueta said that was the moment Leo became “a talking point in and outside of fashion”. Trainer fans were quick to identify Leo’s Nikes as a discontinued retro tennis-style shoe that was first sold in the 70s. “What a papal flex,” declared Esquire , while some online users were quick to christen his style as “holy drip”.
By the end of last year, Leo found himself featured alongside A$AP Rocky and Bad Bunny in Vogue’s best-dressed list, while the New York Times named him as one of its 67 Most Stylish People of 2025.

Orsi said he had been thinking about what the trainers symbolised. “A sportiness? A familiarity with track and field, basketball courts, running?” he pondered. For him it was “a lightness on his feet, a readiness to move quickly to where he is needed the most”, he said. “They signal that he is approachable, like a good coach, and also humble.”

articles.content:
Defending champion arrives at Flushing Meadows in poor form and with a host of challengers looking to usurp her

U nder any normal circumstances Aryna Sabalenka would not have lost her third-round match at the Cincinnati Open last week. For all of her unforced errors, indecisiveness and the obvious tension surrounding her tennis, the world No 1 had led the unheralded Sára Bejlek 5-1 in the first set tie-break and then 4-1 in set two. She gave herself more than enough chances to close out a comfortable win.

Instead Sabalenka returns to New York trying to find a path through her greatest crisis since she first reached No 1 in the rankings more than three years ago. That straight-sets loss in Cincinnati extended a mediocre 17-7 record dating back to the beginning of April during which she has not reached a final. She has just one more chance to turn her fortunes around as she tries to claim her first grand slam title of the year at the US Open, the tournament she has won on the last two occasions.

Such is the competition at the top of women’s tennis, her rivals are congregating at her front door. Elena Rybakina begins this tournament sitting at No 1 in the live standings and in control of her own destiny. Sabalenka must win the title to have any hope of retaining the top ranking, but Rybakina will become the new No 1 regardless of all other results if she reaches the semi-finals. Should either Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to make the semi-finals, they would take top spot. This additional pressure could further add to Sabalenka’s woes, but perhaps, after 97 consecutive weeks as the undisputed best player in the world, this is exactly what she needs.

There are other unanswered questions. Rybakina’s physical condition is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek last week due to a leg injury. A year after she spent this lead-in week to the US Open changing her service action, and parts of her matches in tears, Gauff has rebuilt confidence in her serve and the 2023 champion produced some of her best tennis during her Cincinnati Open title run . Fresh from her own success in Toronto, the 2022 US Open champion Swiatek looks similarly rejuvenated after struggling badly with anxiety and nerves in many matches this year. Pegula, a finalist in Cincinnati having defeated Swiatek, remains as consistent as ever and will put pressure on her rivals.

The strength at the top of women’s game is reflected in the fact that every player inside the top 11 currently holds a WTA 1000 title or above. They have each shown that they are capable of winning the biggest tournaments in the world.

Things could hardly be more different in the men’s draw. As was the case when he exited the French Open in round two, Jannik Sinner’s withdrawal from the US Open with a knee injury has cracked this tournament wide open. Carlos Alcaraz is clearly capable of greatness whenever he enters the court, but the prospect of him launching a serious challenge in his first event back after a four-month layoff due to a right wrist injury and only a few weeks of training seems fanciful. Although he has never been the strongest doubles player, Alcaraz’s rustiness and the caution with which he hit his serve in the mixed doubles competition alongside Serena Williams only reinforced this sentiment.

It was Alexander Zverev who took advantage of the void in Paris to win his first grand slam title and, as the top seed, he is high on the list of contenders again. The two biggest winners in the weeks leading up to the US Open, Montreal and Cincinnati champions Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are young players who have long viewed themselves as worthy of competing for major titles. Such is the cruelty of the draw, the close friends have been drawn to face each other in the fourth round.

Otherwise, just about everyone is in with a shot. The French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli continues to play some of the best tennis of his career, reaching the semi-final in Cincinnati. The rise of 19-year-old Rafael Jódar, who was ranked No 369 this time last year, continues unabated. A group of US players, including Taylor Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien and Brandon Nakashima have found their best form at the right time. Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, will try to replicate the immense level he demonstrated on these courts last year on his run to the semi-final.

Perhaps the most interesting question of all is where Novak Djokovic will land over the next few weeks. Had any of the grand slam tournaments been this wide open in 2025, he would have been heavily favoured to become the oldest champion in history. But a year is an eternity at Djokovic’s advanced age. He has continued to put himself in contention at the grand slams, reaching the Australian Open final and Wimbledon semi-final, but he also has to manage a constant stream of physical problems that only worsen over the course of a fortnight. However, these are not normal circumstances, and he is far from a normal tennis player, so the pursuit of grand slam No 25 is still alive in New York.

articles.title: ‘Special for Norway’: Leknessund breaks clear to win stage seven of Vuelta
articles.summary: Norway in mourning after death of King Harald ‘It’s only a small thing in the bigger picture’ The Norwegian Andreas Leknessund launched a successful solo attack on ⁠the final climb to the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España, ahead of his Uno-X Mobility teammate and compatriot Tobias Johannessen on a day ⁠when their country mourned the death of King Harald . Leknessund made his move from ⁠a five-rider breakaway 7.5km from the finish at ​the end of the ‌149.8km ride from ‌Vall d’Alba, and pulled away to win his first ‌Grand Tour stage on his Vuelta debut. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Norwegian Andreas Leknessund launched a successful solo attack on ⁠the final climb to the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España, ahead of his Uno-X Mobility teammate and compatriot Tobias Johannessen on a day ⁠when their country mourned the death of King Harald .

Leknessund made his move from ⁠a five-rider breakaway 7.5km from the finish at ​the end of the ‌149.8km ride from ‌Vall d’Alba, and pulled away to win his first ‌Grand Tour stage on his Vuelta debut.

“It’s been a special day for the team and also for the whole of Norway,” Leknessund said. “Obviously it’s only a small thing in the bigger picture but still, it ‌makes the day more special.” A minute’s silence was held for King Harald before the stage began in Vall d’Alba, and the Uno-X Mobility team wore black armbands as a mark of respect.

“I didn’t expect it to be this emotional, but for sure there’s so much feelings around this,” Leknessund added. “I’ve ​been fighting really hard, and it means a ‌lot.”

Johannessen came in 34sec behind, having left the Belgian Wout van ​Aert in his wake close to the finish, with the Visma-Lease a Bike rider having to settle for third after he had made the initial attack from the ⁠off and spent most of the day out in ​front with ​Leknessund.

Tadej Pogacar, winner of ​three stages already, was happy to sit ​back in ‌the peloton before ​pulling away ​from his general classification rivals approaching the summit to gain more seconds. The Slovene now leads Spaniard Enric Mas by 3min 50sec.

Van Aert and Leknessund got away early and were joined by ‌another three riders, Johannessen, Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello Q36.5) and Alexey Lutsenko (NSN) coming to the top of the first of five climbs.

The leaders worked together, building a substantial gap and at the foot of the ​final climb the five were one minute ahead of a chasing group of 13 riders with the peloton out of the running with less than 10km to the finish.

Leknessund was the first to try to get away, and when nobody followed he was able to claim his stage win at last, having finished runner-up three times at this year’s Giro d’Italia.

“I said ⁠to Andreas that he should try to go early and then we check if the ​other guys are willing to work together,” ​Johannessen said. “That’s what you always dream about ​when you try to be two guys in the breakaway and you can play it ​like this. I think we ‌played it perfectly.

“A special ​day with what is ​happening back home in Norway so we are super proud.”

Felix Gall, fifth overall, tried to get away from Pogacar, but the Slovene responded and in the end gained 16sec on his closest rival Mas, with Pogacar’s compatriot Primoz Roglic a further minute behind in third.

articles.title: Aston Villa close on Jackson and Mbaye as Emery clears air with departing Watkins
articles.summary: Chelsea’s Jackson and PSG’s Mbaye poised to join Saudi-bound Watkins says sorry for refusing to play Unai Emery said Aston Villa were embarking on a “new chapter” as he prepared to welcome Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson and Paris Saint-Germain’s Ibrahim Mbaye in a near £100m remake of his forward line. Villa are hopeful Jackson will complete his initial £47.5m transfer in time to make his debut at home to Arsenal on Monday and are finalising a move for Mbaye, who will also be about £47m. They needed to reshape up front after accepting a £50m bid from Al-Hilal for Ollie Watkins and are bringing in further funds by selling Emiliano Martínez to Chelsea for £7.5m. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Unai Emery said Aston Villa were embarking on a “new chapter” as he prepared to welcome Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson and Paris Saint-Germain’s Ibrahim Mbaye in a near £100m remake of his forward line.

Villa are hopeful Jackson will complete his initial £47.5m transfer in time to make his debut at home to Arsenal on Monday and are finalising a move for Mbaye, who will also be about £47m. They needed to reshape up front after accepting a £50m bid from Al-Hilal for Ollie Watkins and are bringing in further funds by selling Emiliano Martínez to Chelsea for £7.5m.

Jackson and Mbaye have been longstanding targets for the Villa manager. The 18-year-old winger Mbaye, a Senegal teammate of Jackson, was one of the preferred options to strengthen a key position. He played 24 Ligue 1 games for PSG last season, 10 from the start. In recent days, Villa pushed to sign Rafael Leão from Milan but the Portuguese winger is poised to join Galatasaray, whom Villa will visit in the Champions League.

Jackson was Emery’s No 1 target to replace Watkins, who declined the offer of a new contract in favour of a £50m move to the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal. Both deals are yet to be formally confirmed. The one for Jackson could rise to a club-record £65m with add-ons.

Emery said Watkins’s departure reduced him to tears and he revealed the England striker apologised to him and his teammates for refusing to play in the 4-0 defeat at Brighton last weekend, leaving Villa without a recognised striker.

“I can tell you his commitment and his behaviour was fantastic always,” Emery said. “He told us after the match he was sorry and he told us that he made a mistake, that he was wrong. We accepted it, the players as well, because he always had very good behaviour and commitment with the club, with us and with me.

“For me, he is a fantastic guy, an even more fantastic a guy than a player. I told him bye with a huge hug and a small tear but now it’s a new chapter here with Nicolas Jackson. A new chapter, we replace him and of course all the best to Watkins in Saudi. With Nicolas Jackson replacing him, we are of course happy.”

Emery dismissed the idea that the manner of Watkins’s departure could tarnish his standing among supporters. Watkins is Villa’s record goalscorer in the Premier League era, with 91 goals across 221 league appearances. “The four years working with him have been a high-level relationship with him as a professional,” Emery added. “Last week I was a little bit disappointed. I was disappointed, but we spoke about it, and now clear. One mistake is not closing all the good things he did here. For the supporters as well. He is class, and I think it’s a legacy here.”

Emery said the £50m fees generated for Watkins, who will be 31 in December, and Konsa, who turns 29 in October, were “crazy” given their ages. “We don’t want to be a club to sell players, but the responsibility is to accept it … because for the club it is a good deal. It does not change our objectives.”

Emery acknowledged his side must perform much better against Arsenal than did against Brighton to avoid a second successive defeat. Leon Goretzka, who signed from Bayern Munich on Thursday, could make his debut against the champions, while Zion Suzuki could also feature for the first time after his £30m move from Parma , replacing Martínez.

“Maybe we are not performing like we were performing but the objective is to get to the same way we did, the same performances we had,” said the Villa manager. “We will need time. Last year we showed we needed time. On Monday we will see, [whether] we will need more time or if some players are progressing quickly.”

It promises to be a busy end to the window for Chelsea who, as well as closing in on Martínez, have explored a move for the Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara while they wait for Manchester City to submit their first official offer for Enzo Fernández.

City are yet to make contact with Chelsea over a deal for Fernández, who is desperate to leave before Tuesday night’s deadline. Chelsea are considering their next move and have Camara on a shortlist that also includes Bournemouth’s Alex Scott and Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton. The Senegal international is not seen as a like-for-like replacement for Fernández but would strengthen Xabi Alonso’s midfield options if the Argentina international joins City.

Chelsea are aware of Bournemouth’s determination not to sell Scott and have received similar messages from Palace regarding Wharton, while Arsenal are understood to have knocked back an inquiry for Martín Zubimendi.

Although there have been suggestions that a deal for Fernández will be close to £106.7m, he will only be allowed to leave if Chelsea’s terms are met. Sources have warned City may have to pay more than the west London club’s initial £120m asking price for the 25-year-old.

City are yet to make contact with Chelsea over a deal for Fernández, who is desperate to leave before Tuesday night’s deadline. articles.content:
Readers react to an article by Emine Saner about the arrival of US-style tipping culture in British restaurants and bars

Articles comparing tipping culture in the UK to that in the US ( ‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaos, 24 August ) do not go into the complication of minimum wage calculation in the US. There, wait staff are paid a low base rate, but employers must ensure their earnings are topped up to at least the minimum wage through tips.

As an American who has lived in the UK for 27 years, I have endless discussions with American visiting friends about tipping, and how their example of cultural imperialism has resulted in the distortion of worker value for some of the reasons set out in this article (for example, more attractive people get better tips). The assumption is that people who wait on others don’t have as much money as the tipper, but do we know if this is true? With this logic, should we tip the person who serves us at TK Maxx or Aldi?

Adding to the mix is that the software companies are making money out of us as well. I urge Brits to resist this new trend and press “no tip” on the blasted machine. It’s not about being stingy. If wait staff, or anyone else, are not making a minimum wage, it’s not up to us to subsidise the employer and stump up our earned and taxed pennies to help them out. The onus is on the employer to pay at least the minimum wage, or higher. Pam Foley Oxford

In Japan, soliciting tips has traditionally been seen as begging, and to accept a tip seen as an insult to one’s professional pride. Any business which looked to make tips even quasi-mandatory would be bashed into submission and apology for violating the social norm. (And this is not because service workers are on high wages and wouldn’t benefit from having the tip money, incidentally.)

On our first visit to Australia over 30 years ago we tried to tip the wait person in a diner after a wonderful meal with great service. They quietly admonished us: “You don’t tip here, because we get fair pay.” An egalitarian society where there’s no awkwardness around social status. It’s one of the reasons we decided to stay. Campaign for fair wages, not tips. Jane Pearce Perth, Australia

The one and only time I tried to tip in New Zealand, the taxi driver refused to accept it. Lesley Elliott Auckland, New Zealand

The one that riles me more than anything is the tipping to a charity. “Would you like to donate to …” and the vibe coming from the other side of the counter when you tap no. I will not be told which charities I donate to (I give to local ones where I live), so you can carry on looking as wounded as you like! Alison Maloney Oxford

I was heartened to read your article as I now feel vindicated in my ongoing battle against tipping, when being asked to do so (by a non-smiling staff member) in a local cafe where I am just buying a loaf of bread that I have picked up and put in a bag myself. Jason Beard London

I have never given a tip to anyone. I take the view that I have paid the correct price for the service and that’s an end to the matter. This has caused some embarrassment on the part of my friends and family, but never to me. Shirley Parker-Gore Peasmarsh, East Sussex

Let’s start paying with cash again. It will return control over tipping decisions to customers. Andrew Green St Just, Cornwall

In France, where I live, a restaurant menu is the whole menu and includes tap water, bread, vegetables and indeed the service tip. You can usually see the price before you go in, and unless you want to brag, the correct sum is already on the card machine when this is handed to you for payment. No embarrassing confrontation, no bad surprises. Though if you have received especially attentive service, you can obviously leave a note or coin when you leave. Mette Macrae Mormoiron, France

articles.title: Rob Reiner’s son Jake gives first interview after parents’ deaths: ‘I will never understand why this happened’
articles.summary: Jake says his parents ‘never stopped helping’ his brother Nick, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering both of them at their Los Angeles home Jake Reiner has given his first interview since the killing of his parents, the film-maker Rob Reiner and his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, saying: “I will never understand why this happened.” Reiner, who directed films including The Princess Bride, This Is Spinal Tap and Stand By Me, was found dead alongside Singer Reiner from apparent stab wounds in their home in Los Angeles in December. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Jake says his parents ‘never stopped helping’ his brother Nick, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering both of them at their Los Angeles home

Jake Reiner has given his first interview since the killing of his parents, the film-maker Rob Reiner and his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, saying: “I will never understand why this happened.”

Reiner, who directed films including The Princess Bride, This Is Spinal Tap and Stand By Me, was found dead alongside Singer Reiner from apparent stab wounds in their home in Los Angeles in December.

Their 32-year-old son, Nick Reiner, was indicted for two counts of first-degree murder and has pleaded not guilty.

If he is convicted, he could face the death penalty. Prosecutors have not yet indicated whether they will pursue capital punishment.

Jake and Nick’s sister, Romy Reiner, 28, lived across the street from her parents, and discovered the body of her father.

Speaking to KABC in Los Angeles , Jake Reiner, 35, recalled the moment he heard from his sister after she called 911.

“Romy told me our dad was dead, and then she said, ‘I can’t find mom,’” Reiner said. “I immediately went into shock.

“Our parents had unconditional love for all three of us. I will never understand. I don’t care how it is explained to me, I don’t care what facts come out, I will never understand why this happened,” he said.

“[Nick]’s in jail. It’s like, I physically lost my parents, and then Nick was arrested, now it’s just me and Romy, and we have to navigate this by ourselves essentially,” he said.

“For me, it manifests into anger. It manifests into rage, into how unfair this was, how I didn’t get a say in what happened. I didn’t get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter. I just have to accept the reality of it, and to me, that is just one of the most infuriating parts of all of this.”

Reiner told KABC he had not spoken with his brother and declined to say whether he would want to in the future.

He said his parents “never stopped helping” Nick through his reported struggles with addiction and mental health. The 2015 film Being Charlie, which Nick wrote and Rob directed, was loosely based on Nick’s life.

Reiner added: “The worst kind of grief is your own because you’re the one living through it, and so, just because I lost my parents in the way that I did, it doesn’t mean that you losing a loved one in some other way is not also devastating.

“You can’t compare it, because it’s what you’re going through, and there are a lot of people out there that are living through that, and I think for the first time in my life, I see them.”

He went on to say that the eight months since the deaths had felt like “eight years”, adding: “It also feels like eight minutes because every moment that I wake up, I’m reminded of my reality.”

Reiner wrote a Substack essay about his parents ’ deaths in April, saying the situation was “almost too impossible to process” and “my living nightmare”.

Nick Reiner’s pre-trial hearing for the murder charges is scheduled for 15 September. He has attempted to access $1.6m in a trust his parents set up for him as a child in order to pay his legal fees, but the trust’s professional fiduciary and trustees have blocked him , citing California’s slayer statute, which prevents anyone from financially benefiting from the estate of a person they are accused of killing.

articles.content:
Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’

T he game that graced us with Bathtub Geralt , The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)

As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”

The elephant in the room, though, is that The Witcher 3’s 2016 expansion Blood and Wine felt like a natural conclusion to Geralt’s tale. After decades covered in entrails, the legendary monster slayer hangs up his dual swords for a well-earned life of luxury on his recently acquired vineyard estate. What can he possibly have left to do?

“That is certainly something we thought through,” says Blacha. “Geralt retired in Toussaint – but then his best friend comes calling. I don’t think many of us would turn down that request.”

So, foppish fan favourite Dandelion the bard pulls the witcher back into action, asking Geralt to come to his aid in his homeland of Letten. It’s a seemingly idyllic land of bountiful harvests and rowdy festivals that hides some sinister secrets.

It’s been exciting, and nostalgic. We spent so long with Geralt, but have also learned a lot in the 10-plus years we’ve been away from him,” says Blacha. “With Songs of the Past, we really wanted to return to The Witcher’s roots. That meant drawing on old beliefs and folklore, revisiting landscapes inspired by Poland’s history and countryside, and staying true to the series’ tradition of difficult dilemmas. Going back to all of this has been a pleasure.”

The team has also put to bed rumours that this expansion will be a prequel to The Witcher 4. Songs of the Past is focused on the gruff, grey witcher we’ve already come to love, not Ciri, the younger protagonist of the forthcoming title. Rather, the expansion has all the trappings that seasoned Witcher fans should recognise, with a morally murky narrative brought to life by returning voice actors Doug Cockle and John Schwab, who reprise their roles as Geralt and Dandelion.

There are a few new features to play around with, though: CD Projekt has enhanced Geralt’s combat and skill trees, and he now wields a chain weapon alongside his steel and silver swords. There are also new DNA-modifying mutagens to play around with, tweaking Geralt’s biology and, therefore, his supernatural skills.

The Witcher 3 is a modern classic that has already come to a gratifying end: bringing Geralt out of retirement is a risky move. But when his medallion starts humming, the White Wolf is still ready to answer the call.

articles.content:
Make a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks ahead

W e came up with this when we were looking to create some fun, bespoke but easy-to-serve cocktails that we could pre-batch for busy services but that still had an edge. Vodka is an especially good base for infusions because it’s so neutral, while martinis are having a real moment right now, so this ended up ticking all our boxes, being something that’s recognisable but fun, and also noticeably our own.

articles.content:
News that Scott is working on a follow-up to his maligned 2017 film leaves me worried the franchise has run out of shocks

I f any science-fiction saga looked beyond recovery, it was the Alien franchise. For the 38 years that followed James Cameron’s Aliens, film-makers contrived to find every imaginable way of not making a good Alien film. They tried killing everyone the audience cared about before the opening credits, marooning Sigourney Weaver on a planet populated entirely by bald British character actors , cloning Ripley , pitting xenomorphs against Predators , and sending scientists across the universe to ask an enormous, hairless space bodybuilder why he made them . They even ponied up the thick end of $100m for a film in which Michael Fassbender teaches himself to play the flute .

And then in 2024, we got Fede Álvarez’s Alien: Romulus , in which actual xenomorphs chase actual human beings down actual corridors for the clearly defined purposes of either killing them or putting smaller xenomorphs inside them. Better still, a year later we got Noah Hawley’s Alien: Earth , which reminded us that giant, murderous space insects are in fact less awful than tech trillionaires.

Life was good, but as long-term fans of the franchise, we ought to have known it wouldn’t last. This week, Ridley Scott – who kicked off the entire saga with 1979’s seminal Alien but has yet to make a good sequel or prequel to it – revealed that he is developing a follow-up to his much-maligned 2017 film Alien: Covenant . It would see the return of Fassbender’s David, the murderous android who may or may not have started the ball rolling towards the horrors that eventually became the xenomorphs with his genetic tinkering, and who was last seen steering a colony ship packed with sleeping settlers and human embryos into the great cosmic beyond. According to the 88-year-old film-maker , the new film will detail how David creates, in Scott’s own words, “a brave new world for himself”. Further plot details remain undisclosed, but the British director did helpfully observe that AIs “can go off” and, when they do, are “like a bomb”.

It’s not the first time Scott has talked up sequels to Covenant. During the publicity run for the film, he said a follow-up was already being written and that he would start shooting within 14 months . He also suggested he could make as many as six more Alien prequels, with the series eventually leading up to the original Alien. Eight years and no prequels later, Scott announced that he had “done enough” with the franchise and merely hoped it would continue without him. Now he appears to have reverted to an earlier mode.

Part of the issue is that, alongside season two of Alien: Earth, a sequel to Romulus is already in development. Álvarez and his co-writer Rodo Sayagues have finished the script for the film, which Álvarez will produce (alongside Scott), while another director takes over. That leaves Alien pursuing three different futures at once: Hawley’s corporate small-screen nightmare, the stripped-back survival horror of Romulus, and Scott’s portentous, quasi-theological android opera. Of these three approaches, only one has already been tried twice, to diminishing enthusiasm. Yet Scott apparently remains determined to finish answering questions the franchise is now thriving without. To be fair, Fassbender’s David is one of Alien’s most intriguing antagonists, but he has been the principal attraction in two films that made little case for a third. If we really need to see him again, a high-end television offshoot would surely offer enough room to complete his story. Eight hours ought to be enough for even David to finish explaining himself, and most Alien fans would watch to the end. But another movie in which David quotes poetry and perfects his egg collection while yet another crew of unwitting space colonists inspect it at suicidally close range? That is somewhat more doubtful. There are only so many times you can explain a nightmare before abject terror turns to outright tedium. Give David his limited series, then let the xenomorphs return to the honest work of killing supporting actors in ventilation shafts. In space, nobody needs to hear your origin story.

articles.title: How Katseye became the world’s biggest girl group – while falling apart

articles.content:
Their raucous pop music has made Katseye the biggest girl band in two decades. Can they weather toxic fandom, critical pans and a dwindling member count?

B efore screenings of their new documentary, the members of Katseye appear in a video message to thank fans for their support. Their followers, Eyekons, have played a critical role in their rise to stardom, so it makes sense that Katseye: Wild Hearts , released in global theaters this month, takes a beat to shout out to them. Perhaps more than many other big music groups today, the group’s rise has depended on their relationship with their devotees who ensure that few corners of the world are safe from Katseye mania.

Katseye’s multinational members – Daniela, Lara, Manon, Megan, Sophia and Yoonchae – were selected through a combination of fan votes and judge scores on the 2023 YouTube reality competition The Debut: Dream Academy. The joint project between the American record label Geffen Records and Korean entertainment company Hybe aimed to create a global girl group, with hopefuls participating in a rigorous bootcamp to test their singing and dancing skills. The following year, Netflix’s docu-series Pop Star Academy: Katseye – which documented the group’s nascent era, behind-the-scenes drama and all – catapulted them to a new level of visibility.

Katseye blend western pop’s individualism with the intense training and choreography of the well-oiled K-pop machine. Though they identify as a “global girl group”, much of Katseye’s domination can be credited to their K-pop DNA. “Katseye started with that core K-pop training [and high standards], which ensured they were firing on all cylinders from the start,” said K-pop columnist Jeff Benjamin. “Often in pop, there is a rewarding payoff in seeing an artist finally get backed by a big-label budget for a certain song, music video, or project, but K-pop ensures everything is supported from the start.”

As a $5bn company with offices in Seoul, LA, Mexico City, Tokyo, Miami and Mumbai, Hybe’s resources have certainly contributed to the group’s success, but Katseye don’t adhere to all of K-pop’s structural norms. “There’s no hiding that many top-down decisions are made for them,” said Benjamin. “But Katseye divert by openly speaking about decisions they don’t agree with – the members seem not to like Pop Star Academy and the competition format they were created from – and addressing things most K-pop acts don’t speak about, including their personal lives and sexualities.”

In 2026, Katseye are experiencing a surge of popularity that’s impossible to ignore, including a sold-out tour, nearly 40m monthly Spotify listeners and two Grammy nominations. Katseye: Wild Hearts, which features behind-the-scenes footage, interviews and fan-submitted videos, pulled in nearly $4m its opening weekend. The band have vacuumed up major marketing deals : they’ve worked with State Farm, Pandora, Target and the bougie LA grocery story Erewhon, where they have their own $22 smoothie. Their Gap Better in Denim campaign sparked a wildly viral TikTok trend and saw an upswing in revenue growth for the brand.

Fans in their 20s, teens and younger are eating up what Katseye are serving far beyond retail shelves thanks to their hybrid western pop/K-pop mythos, high-energy performances and inclusive cultural and LGBTQ+ representation. (Two members identify as queer.) There’s also their digital posturing: Katseye is quick to leverage a viral meme to promote their product as well as build relatability with their fans. They reference zoomer Disney Channel nostalgia , collaborate with other chronically online stars such as Troye Sivan and rally fan participation with popular TikTok dances.

“Katseye emerged in a landscape where social media isn’t just a promotional tool, but part of how pop culture is made and circulated,” said Dr Lucy Bennett, senior lecturer in Popular Music and Fandom at Cardiff University. “Fans can take a song, performance or interaction and repackage it for their own social media, promoting the group further.”

In short, the Eyekons are better than any marketing team. “This is particularly significant for a new group because fandom can help create a sense that something is happening around the group, such as a feeling of momentum and cultural relevance.”

Katseye’s core gen Z and Alpha fanbase isn’t by accident. Their easy-to-replicate dance trends, collaborations with toy brands such as Monster High and Gui Gui slime, and “brain rot” lyrics are targeted to young audiences. “Boba tea (gnarly) / Tesla (gnarly) / Fried chicken (gnarly),” they sing on Gnarly, while their latest single features lines such as: “Carry my matcha / Mount Valley water / I like my mochi drenched in chocolata.”

The group’s fast-tracked success has not come without friction. Katseye say they have faced “heavy” racist and sexist harassment, dealt with extreme toxic fandom and received death threats. Lara, a Connecticut-raised US citizen of Tamil Indian background, told the BBC she was falsely reported to ICE, while Sophia, who is Filipina-American, revealed their family members had received hateful comments. Manon, who is of Swiss-Ghanaian heritage, called the experience “terrorizing on the mind”.

Like the Pussycat Dolls, Fifth Harmony and other girl groups before them, Katseye have faced an onslaught of rumors of tensions within the group. Shadily edited clips of the girls have been presented on social media as proof of enmity between members. Some have outright pitted the girls against each other. “People see us as women to rank. They’ll grade us based on how pretty we are, our singing skill, dancing skill, and then add it up and give us a percentage. That’s so dystopian,” Lara said.

The all-too-familiar parasocial expectations fans have of artists weigh heavily over Katseye, but that’s nothing new in pop. “The more intimate the digital relationship becomes, the more complicated it can be to maintain boundaries,” said Bennett. “Because fans can invest so much time and emotional energy in an artist, this can create expectations around access and responsiveness.”

Other public scrutiny surrounding the band has been murkier. In February, the group announced Manon was taking a temporary step back to “focus on her health and wellbeing”, leaving the band to perform at Coachella as a five-piece. Soon after, she removed references to Katseye from her Instagram bio.

In August, just months after Manon stepped back, Hybe announced Sophia was similarly going on hiatus for her “mental health and wellness”, casting another shadow of uncertainty over the group’s seemingly dwindling roster. It’s unclear if she will return in time to join her bandmates on their global Wildworld Tour this September. Meanwhile, the active members have voiced their support for both bandmates during recent promotional activities and appearances. Bennett said “the participatory nature of Katseye’s formation” makes their relationship with fans complex. “If fans have voted, promoted, defended and helped shape the formation of the group, they may feel they have a genuine stake in what happens to it. That can be a really positive thing, creating a strong sense of loyalty and investment in the group. At the same time, fans may feel that their investment gives them a particular interest in questioning or discussing decisions about [the band].”

Katseye’s trajectory has so far triumphed over hiatuses, controversies and sneery rumors. Released on 14 August, Wild is a mega-success. The EP debuted at No 1 on the Billboard 200, setting a remarkable new record for the biggest week by a girl group in the streaming era. Wild also marks the biggest US debut for a girl group since Danity Kane’s 2008 album Welcome to the Dollhouse, and is the fourth No 1 album by a girl group this decade following K-pop releases such as Blackpink’s Born Pink, NewJeans’ second EP Get Up, and Twice’s With You-th. Despite record-breaking sales, critics are less enthused about the band’s recent output. Vulture called Wild a “war between bittersweet pop … and deliberately juvenile singles”, while Pitchfork shrugged at its “hollow” songs. Perhaps a testament to their rebellious gen Z pop swag, Katseye refuse to be chained to any one rhythm in particular – for better or worse.

When the EP bangs, it bangs: Pinky Up , the spiritual successor to the initially polarizing Gnarly, is an intoxicating blast of thumping techno-pop. Co-penned by Ed Sheeran , Animal is a slice of radio-primed, early-2010s throwback pop. Tragically, one of the EP’s best songs, Unloveu, is a Target physical CD exclusive. Written by Lara, the ballad highlights the individual members’ voices as they harmonize about recovering from a toxic relationship. It hints at what could be if Katseye’s artistic input and vocals were emphasized above viral choreography and brand endorsements. Wild’s sonic incohesiveness and genre-hopping make for an uneven listening experience. It’s also woefully devoid of standout solo moments, the girls’ voices often blending into a sleek but frustratingly symmetrical monovocal. Bel Air, an unreleased 13-year-old Charli xcx song, is so languid it sounds more like a raw demo than the original. Then there’s Hootie Frutti. The Brazilian funk-flavored single is the EP’s most divisive, with some celebrating its chaotic, campy silliness and others criticizing its sexually charged, comedically product placement-heavy music video. (Manon and Sophia might be on hiatus. Orange-flavored Tic Tacs are decidedly not.)

Amid a whiplash-inducing string of brand deals and promotions, fans are worried Katseye are being overworked. Maybe so. Representatives for the band did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment for this article. K-pop has long been under scrutiny for its infamously intense work schedules, while the western pop industry is no better for the many pressures facing female artists in particular. Coupled with various health-related hiatuses and public controversies, a cloudy patina of skepticism lies over the group’s nonstop schedules. In the past two weeks alone they have performed at the Disney Legends awards, appeared on the Today Show and Tonight Show, performed a Spotify event called Klub Katseye, signed CDs at Hot Topic and Barnes & Noble and headlined a music festival.

Katseye’s potential for mainstream pop staying power is undeniable. As the global pop group of today, they are heralded by fans for their confidence, vibrant and distinct personalities – they embody an attitude emblematic of modern sisterhood in all its messy, magical glory – and celebration of diversity and digital culture. But something feels unsustainable. While one demand of the pop industry seems to be maintaining momentum at all costs, Katseye’s grueling commitments coupled with unrelenting public scrutiny could be harmful in the long run. Nonstop activity could also be holding the group back from more intentionally developing their core image and artistic perspective – both paramount to solidifying a musical legacy outside of flash-in-the-pan trends.

Time will tell if the band’s current hyper-saturation is a natural outcome of the well-earned hype surrounding them, or a consequence of a larger, more insidious system that views pop stars as products. Perhaps after the Wild promotion is done, the band would benefit from a collective recalibration to figure out what artistic goals exist for Katseye beyond going viral. These talented performers deserve as much.

Soon after, she removed references to Katseye from her Instagram bio.

In August, just months after Manon stepped back, Hybe announced Sophia was similarly going on hiatus for her “mental health and wellness”, casting another shadow of uncertainty over the group’s seemingly dwindling roster. It’s unclear if she will return in time to join her bandmates on their global Wildworld Tour this September. Meanwhile, the active members have voiced their support for both bandmates during recent promotional activities and appearances. Bennett said “the participatory nature of Katseye’s formation” makes their relationship with fans complex. “If fans have voted, promoted, defended and helped shape the formation of the group, they may feel they have a genuine stake in what happens to it. That can be a really positive thing, creating a strong sense of loyalty and investment in the group. At the same time, fans may feel that their investment gives them a particular interest in questioning or discussing decisions about [the band].”

Katseye’s trajectory has so far triumphed over hiatuses, controversies and sneery rumors. Released on 14 August, Wild is a mega-success. The EP debuted at No 1 on the Billboard 200, setting a remarkable new record for the biggest week by a girl group in the streaming era. Wild also marks the biggest US debut for a girl group since Danity Kane’s 2008 album Welcome to the Dollhouse, and is the fourth No 1 album by a girl group this decade following K-pop releases such as Blackpink’s Born Pink, NewJeans’ second EP Get Up, and Twice’s With You-th. Despite record-breaking sales, critics are less enthused about the band’s recent output. Vulture called Wild a “war between bittersweet pop … and deliberately juvenile singles”, while Pitchfork shrugged at its “hollow” songs. Perhaps a testament to their rebellious gen Z pop swag, Katseye refuse to be chained to any one rhythm in particular – for better or worse.

When the EP bangs, it bangs: Pinky Up , the spiritual successor to the initially polarizing Gnarly, is an intoxicating blast of thumping techno-pop. Co-penned by Ed Sheeran , Animal is a slice of radio-primed, early-2010s throwback pop. Tragically, one of the EP’s best songs, Unloveu, is a Target physical CD exclusive. Written by Lara, the ballad highlights the individual members’ voices as they harmonize about recovering from a toxic relationship. It hints at what could be if Katseye’s artistic input and vocals were emphasized above viral choreography and brand endorsements. Wild’s sonic incohesiveness and genre-hopping make for an uneven listening experience. It’s also woefully devoid of standout solo moments, the girls’ voices often blending into a sleek but frustratingly symmetrical monovocal. Bel Air, an unreleased 13-year-old Charli xcx song, is so languid it sounds more like a raw demo than the original. Then there’s Hootie Frutti. The Brazilian funk-flavored single is the EP’s most divisive, with some celebrating its chaotic, campy silliness and others criticizing its sexually charged, comedically product placement-heavy music video. (Manon and Sophia might be on hiatus. Orange-flavored Tic Tacs are decidedly not.)

Amid a whiplash-inducing string of brand deals and promotions, fans are worried Katseye are being overworked. Maybe so. Representatives for the band did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment for this article. K-pop has long been under scrutiny for its infamously intense work schedules, while the western pop industry is no better for the many pressures facing female artists in particular. Coupled with various health-related hiatuses and public controversies, a cloudy patina of skepticism lies over the group’s nonstop schedules. In the past two weeks alone they have performed at the Disney Legends awards, appeared on the Today Show and Tonight Show, performed a Spotify event called Klub Katseye, signed CDs at Hot Topic and Barnes & Noble and headlined a music festival.

Katseye’s potential for mainstream pop staying power is undeniable. As the global pop group of today, they are heralded by fans for their confidence, vibrant and distinct personalities – they embody an attitude emblematic of modern sisterhood in all its messy, magical glory – and celebration of diversity and digital culture. But something feels unsustainable. While one demand of the pop industry seems to be maintaining momentum at all costs, Katseye’s grueling commitments coupled with unrelenting public scrutiny could be harmful in the long run. Nonstop activity could also be holding the group back from more intentionally developing their core image and artistic perspective – both paramount to solidifying a musical legacy outside of flash-in-the-pan trends.

Time will tell if the band’s current hyper-saturation is a natural outcome of the well-earned hype surrounding them, or a consequence of a larger, more insidious system that views pop stars as products. Perhaps after the Wild promotion is done, the band would benefit from a collective recalibration to figure out what artistic goals exist for Katseye beyond going viral. These talented performers deserve as much.

articles.summary: New Guardian Food show FEED with Jimi Famurewa travels the UK in search of food trends. This hearty dish is his homemade twist on a takeaway favourite The chicken here – which is roasted rather than breaded and fried – might confuse some spice bag purists, but the Filipino-inspired spice bag at Lasa in Belfast (barbecued chicken and a calamansi and coconut milk red curry sauce) showed me that other elements can be added to this Irish-Chinese takeaway classic.
